THE PANZER CAPTAIN AMERICA 

Known as 'Captain America', the Harley-Davidson chopper ridden by Peter Fonda in the iconic movie Easy Rider is one of the most readily identifiable motorcycles ever made. Since the movie's release in 1968 there have been countless replicas made, usually by individual customizers or enthusiasts, but a few years ago an American motorcycle manufacturer decided to put its own version into limited production. In creating their 'Captain America' replica, Panzer Motorcycle Works was able to call on the resources of a sizeable industry of engine and component manufacturers devoted to producing their own Harley-style motors. Panzer's 90ci (1,500cc) Neo-Pan unit is sourced from specialist engine builders, Accurate Engineering of Dohan, Alabama and incorporates crankcases, crankshaft, rods, cylinders and pistons from S&S, and STD cylinder heads. 

The frame and most of the cycle parts come from Paughco, so it made sense for the Captain to be assembled by them rather than at Panzer's factory in Canyon City, Colorado. Almost inevitably, there have been some departures from the original movie bike's specification, Panzer's version incorporating a RevTech five-speed gearbox, belt final drive, disc brakes and an electric starter in the interests of improved performance and practicality, as well as other changes to conform with Federal traffic laws.

One of reputedly only 50 made, this Panzer Captain was purchased by the current owner in Europe and having made its way back to the states in the past few years. THE HARLEY-DAVIDSON FL 

The FL was introduced to the Harley-Davidson model line in 1941. It used a 74ci version of the "Knucklehead" OHV engine; the EL a 61ci version. The FL and EL shared the same frame, and with the U and UL, which used a 74ci flathead engine. The FL replaced the UH and ULH using the same frame but with an 80ci flathead engine. And then the FL continued relatively unchanged until 1948, when it (with the EL) was given redesigned "Panhead" engines of the same capacities, 74ci and 61ci, respectively, as before. These engines now include self-adjusting hydraulic lifters and aluminum cylinder heads to reduce weight and improve cooling. The U and UL flathead twins were discontinued in 1948, leaving the OHV EL and FL models as Harley-Davidson's large-frame, large capacity, highly stylized motorcycles. 

Few films encapsulated the 1960s in the same way the Easy Rider did. Released July 14th, 1969, it was met with immediate commercial success being the 4th top grossing film of 1969. Its cultural impact was much farther reaching and long lasting. The movie follows two characters Billy and Wyatt as they ride from Los Angeles to Mardi Gras in Louisianna. Intertwined with Peter Fonda's and Dennis Hopper's characters are the choppers they ride. Built by Ben Hardy, who was a pioneer African American southern California Chopper builder, in conjunction with civil rights activist Cliff Vaughn. Using late 1940s former LAPD service motorcycles as a basis for the bikes Ben and Cliff created two characters that immediately became part of the 1960s counter culture lexicon. None of the original bikes survive today, and as such almost immediately people were reproducing these two characters. 

THE MOTORCYCLE OFFERED 

An extremely true-to-form example, utilizing a period 1954 Harley FL engine, 4 speed ratchet top gear box, and wishbone frame, this Billy Bike is as though it leapt off the screen. The machine on offer here was also signed by the actor who plays Billy, the late Dennis Hopper. This example has resided in a stable of other incredible Harley's for years and is being offered for sale for the first time since its construction. This Billy Bike presents a rare opportunity to own a truly iconic piece of film history. Truly an American icon, it would be a welcome addition to any mechanical collection.

It was also the final season for the dramatic "skeg" tailfins introduced in 1961 â slim, blade-like fins that housed the tail lamps and gave the big convertible a sense of motion even at rest, before the cleaner, more restrained lines of the all-new 1963 body arrived. Styled under the direction of GM's Bill Mitchell, the 1962 Eldorado struck a careful balance between the excess of the late-1950s fin era and the crisper formality that would follow and is regarded by many collectors as the most cohesively styled Cadillac of the period.

THE BUICK MODEL 65 SPORT PHAETON

Introduced during one of the most challenging periods in American automotive history, the 1932 Buick Model 65 Sport Phaeton exemplified Buick's commitment to engineering excellence and refined craftsmanship. The Model 65 combined effortless performance with innovative features such as GM's new Synchro-Mesh transmission, Ride Control adjustable shock absorbers, and the Wizard Control vacuum-assisted clutch system. The elegant Sport Phaeton body was among Buick's rarest offerings, with only 79 domestic examples produced.

THE CAR OFFERED

One of the few known surviving Model 65 Sport Phaetons, chassis 2644092 has remained in the same long-term ownership for many decades and underwent a comprehensive restoration, completed in 1997. The car eventually did change hands around 2019 and has been living in sunny California since. Finished in two-tone brown with green pinstriping and matching green spoke wheels, the car retains numerous desirable factory options, including dual side-mounted spares, luggage rack, leather interior and superbly worked wood dash inserts with clock, 90-mph speedometer and gauges for fuel level, amperage, oil pressure, and water temperature. Restoration work included a replacement honeycomb radiator, replating the brightwork, new ash top bows, new canvas top, running boards and woodgrain dashboard panels. To improve reliability a spin-on oil filter, auxiliary fuel pump and battery cut-off switch were added and sealed bearings replaced the stock fan tension pulley bushing while the fuel pre-heater was disconnected. A new fuel tank was installed in 2012, the Marvel carburetor was rebuilt in 2014 and new rear brakes fitted in 2017. 

This rare and beautifully presented Buick comes with some service records, manuals, brochures and represents an outstanding example of one of the marque's most distinctive and seldom-seen prewar touring automobiles.

THE BANCROFT

Introduced in 1991, the Bancroft Roadster was the creation of American racing driver and designer Hugh Bancroft, who set out to reinterpret the elegant, long-hooded roadsters of the 1930s through the lens of contemporary German engineering.

Production was entrusted to GFG-Exklusiv-Cars GmbH of Gronau, Westphalia â the same specialist coachworks responsible for the equally rare Elisar â and each car was completed under the patronage of Graf and GrÃ¤fin Beissel von Gymnich, whose name lent the project both cachet and continuity with Germany's coachbuilding tradition. Although a limited series of 300 cars was originally announced, commercial realities intervened, and production halted after around just ten examples had been built between 1991 and 1993, at a new price of between DM 300,000 and DM 396,000 â a sum that placed the Bancroft firmly among the most expensive German cars of its day.

Beneath its traditionally styled aluminum and steel coachwork, the Bancroft was thoroughly modern. Power was delivered by a 5.0-litre OHC derived from Mercedes-Benz running gear mated to a four-speed automatic transmission with driver-selectable sport and economy modes. A lambda-controlled three-way catalytic converter ensured the car met the emissions standards of the day without compromising the effortless, long-legged character for which its donor powertrain was known.

THE CAR OFFERED

This example is offered by only its second private owner, having reportedly been acquired directly from Hugh Bancroft's family. Their personal Bancroft remained in their climate-controlled private garage in Costa Mesa, California for approximately twenty-five to thirty years before its sale to the current vendor â a long period of static, indoor storage that goes some way toward explaining the car's exceptional originality and notably low recorded mileage. At the time of purchase the family reportedly still retained what appeared to be a full-size wooden styling buck associated with the Bancroft project, together with several original transport crates and related ephemera that had remained with the collection for decades further reinforcing the provenance of this particular Bancroft.

With a total production run in the single digits, this Bancroft Roadster represents a rare opportunity to acquire a genuine, well-preserved piece of low-volume German coachbuilding history â a car engineered with the substance of a Mercedes-Benz and dressed with the romance of a 1930s Grand Tourer.

THE JAGUAR XK120

Conceived and constructed in just a few months, the XK120 debuted at the 1948 Earls Court Motor Show where the stunning-looking roadster caused a sensation, the resulting demand for what was then the world's fastest production car taking Jaguar by surprise. 

Its stunning appearance notwithstanding, the XK120 was conventional enough beneath the skin, being built on a separate chassis featuring independent front suspension by means of wishbones and torsion bars, a live rear axle and drum brakes all round. The car's heart was, of course, the fabulous XK engine. Intended for Jaguar's post-war range-topping saloon, the 3.4-liter six embodied the best of modern design, boasting twin overhead camshafts running in an aluminum-alloy cylinder head, seven main bearings and a maximum output of 160bhp. When installed in the lightweight XK120, the result was a car with a phenomenal power-to-weight ratio and blistering performance. 

The XK120 set new standards of comfort, handling and performance for sports cars and in keeping with the Jaguar tradition there was nothing to touch it at the price. Coupe and Drophead Coupe versions followed, which provided the opportunity to offer a luxurious interior with copious amounts of wood veneer. Regardless of the type of bodywork, the XK120 was a genuine 120mph car capable of sustained high-speed cruising. 

THE CAR OFFERED

This beautiful XK120 Roadster - or Open Two-Seater as officially called in the day - first roared to life inside Jaguar's Coventry facility on August 31st, 1950. Originally finished in Birch Grey over a Biscuit and Red interior and Frech Grey convertible top, this left-hand drive Roadster was destined for the American market to where it was dispatched on September 7th, 1950. Initially distributed by East Coast agent Max Hoffman in New York City, the car was sold to its first owner through Geo J Lenz Automobiles in Niagara Falls, New York.

Retaining its original engine, the Jaguar was subsequently restored and refinished in red. The black leather interior was retrimmed in 2015âincluding new hides, carpets, and dashâat a reported cost of $8,000, but no receipts are included. Driveability improvements include 12-volt electronics, uprated cooling system with an electric fan, and a set of new Firestone tires that were fitted in March of this year.

Documented by its Jaguar Daimler Heritage Trust Certificate and a selection of service records, it is a lovely machine that would make a fine tour vehicle for its next lucky owner.

THE LANCIA AURELIA

Introduced in 1907, Vincenzo Lancia's first car showed an independence of thought and defiance of convention that would remain associated with the marque well into the modern era. Lancia recommenced production after WWII with the Aprilia and its smaller cousin the Ardea but waiting in the wings was yet another groundbreaking design: the Aurelia. Lancia's classic Aurelia, the first car ever to employ a V6 engine, was launched at the 1950 Turin Motor Show. Designed in wartime by Francesco de Virgilio, the 1,754cc 60-degree V6 was of all-aluminum construction and used overhead valves operated via short pushrods instead of Lancia's traditional overhead camshafts. An advanced unitary-construction design, the Aurelia retained Lancia's 'sliding pillar' independent front suspension, first seen on the Lambda, but used a novel semi-trailing-arm layout at the rear, another world first. The transmission too, was unusual, comprising a two-piece prop-shaft and combined gearbox/rear transaxle on which were mounted the inboard brakes, though for once this was not an entirely new departure. 

The B10 saloon was joined the following year by the Pinin Farina-styled B20 GT Coupe, a fastback '2+2' on a shortened wheelbase which, with its combination of sports car performance and saloon car practicality, can be said to have introduced the Gran Turismo concept to the world. The Aurelia engine had been increased to 1,991cc in 1951 and it was this unit in up-rated form that went into the B20 GT. Lighter and higher geared than the saloon, the B20 GT was good for a top speed of over 100mph. An engineering tour de force clothed in sublime coachwork by Italy's foremost carrozzeria, the Aurelia B20 represents for many the zenith of Lancia's post-war production. 

Stunning the motor racing world, a mildly race-developed B20 GT driven by chain-smoking, brandy-swigging Giovanni Bracco finished 2nd in the 1951 Mille Miglia, beaten only by Luigi Villoresi's 4.1-liter works Ferrari! It is worth noting that the nimble Aurelia was actually faster than the Ferrari over the mountain passes north of Florence. Sharing his Aurelia B20 GT with Umberto Maglioli, Bracco won the Targa Florio for Lancia in 1952 and in 1954 another B20 won the Monte Carlo Rally in the hands of the famous Monegasque driver Louis Chiron.

6th Series Lancia B20 GTs featured all the refinements and improvements developed on the earlier iterations of the superbly engineered and manufactured Aurelia Coupes. The 2.5-liter engine delivered more performance than ever. A stronger transaxle and De Dion suspension helped to maintain excellent balance and an exquisite driving experience.

According to the copy of the Lancia Registro Aurelia on file, this example was assembled at the end of May 1958 and tested prior to shipment on July 30, 1958. Originally finished in Grigio Chiaro. over grey cloth, the car has subsequently been restored in its original exterior color and retrimmed with red leather. Acquired by the current owner in 2023, it appears has been well kept and actively enjoyed and includes highly desirable features including left-hand drive (the 'S' standing for 'sinistra' â Italian for left), a Nardi Kit for a bit more power, and a floor-mounted manual transmission. Carefully maintained and regularly driven, it has been a participant on multiple rally events, including the Tejas Turismo, where it is reported by the vendor to have been gleefully enjoyed without issue.

Complete with the aforementioned Lancia Registro Aurelia, original marketing material, English instruction book, magazines, and some service records, it would make an excellent addition to just about any collection. Eligible for countless events and a delight to drive, a Lancia Aurelia is a necessary addition to just about any car collection â and this example would be among the most enjoyable out there.

THE FERRARI 365GT 2+2

Once the 250 GTE entered production in 1960, Ferrari's line of four-seat Grand Tourers rapidly became the marque's best-selling models. Fast, handsome and eminently practical, they faced little in the way of competition until the arrival of the Lamborghini Espada in 1968. By that time Ferrari had already launched its third-generation four-seater, the 365 GT, successor to the 330 GT which had in turn superseded the original 250 GTE.

Presented at the Paris Motor Show in October 1967, the 365 GT was the largest and most spacious road car Ferrari had yet produced. Built on a new Tipo 591 tubular steel chassis, it introduced fully independent suspension to Ferrari's four-seat V12 line for the first time, in place of the live rear axle used by its predecessors. Unequal-length wishbones and coil-sprung telescopic dampers were fitted at each corner, the rear axle benefiting from a hydraulic self-levelling system developed in conjunction with Koni to maintain a consistent ride height regardless of load or speed. Power steering, previously the preserve of the flagship 365 California, was standardised across the range, while a new twin-circuit hydraulic braking system with ventilated discs replaced the solid units of the 330 GT.

Styled by Pininfarina in the idiom of the earlier 330 GTC Speciale but with a more cost-effective fastback rear screen in place of that car's compound-curved glass, the 365 GT's steel bodyshell â aluminum hood and trunk lid apart â clothed a cabin trimmed to a very high standard: full leather upholstery, electric windows, an oval instrument binnacle behind a wood-rimmed wheel, and a teak-faced console housing the clock, fuel gauge and ammeter. Options included air conditioning, a radio, Borrani wire wheels and Plexiglass headlamp covers.

Power came from a 4,390cc all-alloy, single-overhead-camshaft V12 of Colombo lineage, fed by three twin-choke Weber 40 DFI/5 carburetors and producing a claimed 320bhp at 6,600rpm and 268lb ft at 5,000rpm â sufficient for a top speed of 152mph and 0-62mph in under seven seconds. Drive was taken through a conventional five-speed manual gearbox and ZF limited-slip differential; a small number of cars destined for the North American market, at the request of Ferrari's importer Luigi Chinetti, were instead fitted with a General Motors three-speed automatic.

Production of the 365 GT ran for three and a half years, ending in early 1971 with the introduction of the Pininfarina-styled 365 GT4 2+2 at the Geneva Motor Show. In that time 806 cars were completed with chassis numbers running from 11051 to 14099, preceded by six pre-production prototypes.

Acquired by the current owner in 1987, it has been cherished and used in Ferrari Club of America events from the 1990s up to the present.

The engine was rebuilt in 2004 by the respected Californian marque specialist Allen S. Bishop, author of the Ferrari Guide to Performance and a noted concours judge at Pebble Beach and other major events over a long career devoted to the marque. Invoices and correspondence relating to this work are retained within the accompanying comprehensive history file. Additionally, after correspondence with noted historian Marcel Massini, the owner commissioned a repaint from Black back to the original Blue Turbillon in 2015. The odometer currently displays 75,342 miles.

Presented as a sorted, ready-to-enjoy driver rather than a trailer queen, this 365 GT wears its history honestly and runs and drives as a well-sorted example of the model should. It is a genuinely handsome car in the metal â the Pininfarina lines have aged gracefully, and the proportions read as elegant rather than merely large, drawing admiring glances at every fuel stop. For a buyer who wants to use a four-seat V12 Ferrari rather than simply own one, it would be hard to find a more usable, better-sorted example.

THE CAR OFFERED

By some way one of the most admired and best-respected of all great American racing drivers is the late, multi-talented Dan Gurney. Right here Bonhams is delighted to offer one of the great sportsman's most rare winning cars - the Lola-Ford T70 Spyder in which he scored the only win ever achieved with a Ford V8 engine in the international Canadian-American Challenge Cup race series.

Dan drove this beautifully proportioned, elegant Lola to victory in the second CanAm round ever held, the inaugural 1966 series' Round 2, run on the 2.85-mile Bridgehampton circuit on Long Island, USA. 

There Dan faced formidable opposition. It included a pair of sister Lola T70s: one the quasi-works Team Surtees entry for former Ferrari F1 World Champion Driver (and seven-times World Champion motorcycle rider) John Surtees, the other a Roger Penske-entered variant driven by another great, Mark Donohue. And there's more. The opposition to Gurney's car was strengthened immensely by two works Chaparrals running with tall strutted wings above their rear decks, for constructor Jim Hall and 1961 F1 World Champion Phil Hill, while a pair of lightweight new Elva-McLaren works cars appeared in the hands of that year's Ford Le Mans 24-Hour race winners, Bruce McLaren and Chris Amon. After suffering wing problems in practice pole winner Jim Hall withdrew for race day, Dan Gurney then starting from pole in this Lola-Ford T70 Spyder, entered by his AAR team. 

As contemporary race reporter Ruth Sands Bentley wrote in the British journal Autosport the following week: "Dan Gurney drove brilliantly and steadily to win the Bridgehampton 200 Miles race for the Canadian-American Challenge. He took the lead at the outset and never lost it. His average speed for the 70 laps was 105.58mph, a new record, and his victory gave him nine points towards the CanAm Challenge Cup. His car" - she confirmed - "was an all-American Racers Lola T70 powered by the 5.3-liter Gurney Weslake-Ford unit".

She went on to relate how at the race's mid-point Dan Gurney had led from Phil Hill's Chaparral and the twin works McLarens of Bruce himself and his young New Zealand compatriot Chris Amon. But: "On lap 52 Hill and Amon passed as one car, and the next lap Amon was in second place - chasing - the Californian over the finishing line, only half a second and 30 feet separating the two cars at the chequered flag. Dan in the Lola-Ford left the lap record at a new mark of 108.88mph."

However, this stand-out performance was not to be repeated in the rest of that year's inaugural series, as Dan subsequently retired from every round - despite it being a sister Lola T70, John Surtees's Chevrolet V8-powered version, which ultimately took that year's CanAm Championship title.

This car had actually been invoiced and delivered to legendary racing personality, entrepreneur and agent Carroll Shelby for Gurney's All-American Racers team use on June 8, 1966. In initial form it was liveried in black, matching Gurney's famous crash helmet, but it was rapidly re-painted in dark blue and white, very much becoming one of AAR's first 'Eagles'.

Carroll Shelby was actually a partner of Gurney's in AAR, sponsored jointly by Goodyear Tires and - for their engine program - by the Ford Motor Company. Further backing for the CanAm program came from Bardahl. Dan, meanwhile, was having his own 3-liter V12 Formula 1 engine developed for him in the UK by Harry Weslake Research Limited, renowned exports in engine combustion and gas-flow matters. 

While that initial 1966 season and series concluded with more engine unreliability than would have been hoped, Dan effectively presented the car to his ex-Shelby protÃ©gÃ© Swede Savage in preparation for 1967. Savage proved very quick as an aspiring young driver, but was to die tragically in a fiery accident at Indianapolis during the 1973 500-Miles race, while driving a George Bignotti-entered Eagle-Offenhauser.

Meanwhile this Lola T70 Spyder lay unused until 1968 when it featured in a Riverside Raceway movie film session for the Paul Newman, Joanne Woodward and Robert Wagner feature Winning. Later that year it was sold to Eric Hauser, who offered it as a rent-a-drive CanAm mount, but failed to find any takers.

Hauser and Doug Hooper instead ran it themselves, entering the 1968 Stardust Grand Prix at Las Vegas, and the Monterey and Los Angeles Times (Riverside) GPs in 1969. In the early 1970s it was bought by Bobby Thompson of Houma, Louisiana, then passed on to his son Bobbie Thompson in New Orleans. He rapidly sold it to Charlie Bartz who ran the car in Bonsai Club events while retaining it into 1982. 

This important Dan Gurney car had by then had its history largely obscured by the passage of time. Even so, it was acquired by Bobby Hogg of Georgia who used it mainly for show and display until 1985. A leaking fuel cell then persuaded him to put it into store in a chicken coop near the Road Atlanta circuit, where it remained for the following twenty years until acquired by the current owner in 2005. The new keeper then painstakingly restored this important car through 2006 and he was then invited to drive it in the 2007 Goodwood Festival of Speed event in England. It has since been used regularly for such demonstration events while spending much of its time on museum or collection display - including the Rolex Monterey Motorsports Reunion, plus Concours at Road America and Carmel, California. It has been invited for display at Amelia Island, Sebring, St Joliet Raceway, and of course back to the scene of its 1966 triumph at Bridgehampton - while in 2018 we understand that it actually featured as the pace car for the Rolex 24-Hours race at Daytona.

This beautiful mid-'60s sports-racing Lola with its stressed-skin monocoque chassis and exquisitely-styled bodywork by Specialised Mouldings of England was ahead of its time when new. It bucked the trend in Gurney preferring Ford V8 to Chevrolet V8 power then - and in effect rocked the establishment by winning for 'The Oval' at Bridgehampton.

A fascinating file of historical documentation and photography accompanies this handsome car and as a Dan Gurney CanAm race winner - and indeed as Ford's only CanAm race winner - it shares remarkably significant twin claims to historic prominence. 

We recommend it highly to the market as deserving the most serious consideration... Beauty, connection, history - even a Hollywood movie industry link - Lola T70 'SL71/34' here just about offers it all.

THE PORSCHE SPEEDSTER

As Porsche's official importer to the United States, Max Hoffman recognized that the American market wanted something leaner and racier than the standard 356. His answer, introduced in 1954, was the Speedster: stripped of superfluous weight, fitted with a low, raked and easily removable windshield, lightweight bucket seats and a minimal folding top with side curtains. The result weighed nearly 200 pounds less than the coupe and was correspondingly quicker, and it was an immediate success on both road and track.

With the arrival of the 356 A in 1955 came the enlarged 1,582cc engine, and with it the option of the Type 616/2 Super unit. Rated at 75bhp against the standard 60, the Super transformed the Speedster from a spirited road car into a genuinely competitive one. Only 645 examples of the 1600 Super Speedster were built in 1956, the $500 premium over the standard car being, in the parlance of the day, what separated the men from the boys.

THE CAR OFFERED

Chassis 82311 was originally delivered April 5, 1957 through Hoffman Motor Cars to the American market as a white over black "Super" Speedster optioned with US gauges and sealed beam headlights. Reportedly the Speedster spent the first fifteen years of its life exactly as its maker intended: racing in SCCA competition as many other Speedsters did when new. No trace of that hard-fought early career remains today, however, the car having been the subject of an exacting restoration by the widely respected late Porsche specialist Gary Kempton of Crawfordville, Florida in the early 2000s.

Conceived as Kempton's own testament to the marque and executed with a series of subtle but effective upgrades, the car is finished in shimmering Adria Blue over a contrasting gray leather interior. While at first glance it might appear a beautifully presented but otherwise standard Speedster, closer inspection reveals its finer points. Beneath the engine lid, the later 356 SC sourced hot-rodded air cooled flat four, recently serviced by renowned Porsche mechanics Scott's Independent of Anaheim, California, gives a healthy shove of torque and about 95 horsepower. Transferring this power to the road is a later Type 741 356 C derived gearbox. The candle-like lighting provided by the original 6-volt system has been replaced by a more reliable 12 volt system, and the interior has been upgraded to gray leather. Completing the elegant look, this Speedster rides on a brand-new set of reproduction Rudge knock-off wheels. 

Following its restoration, the car has passed through a succession of knowledgeable Porsche enthusiasts and has been widely profiled appearing on the cover of 356 Registry magazine and being featured in 911 & Porsche World. It is accompanied by the Rudge wheel knock-off tool, a set of side curtains, and photographic documentation of the restoration conducted by Gary Kempton.

A desirable Super Speedster restored to an exceptional standard by one of the marque's most admired specialists, chassis 82311 represents an outstanding opportunity to acquire one of the most charismatic sporting Porsches of the 1950s.

THE MASERATI GHIBLI

Introduced at the 1966 Turin Motor Show as a concept car, the Maserati Ghibli immediately established itself among the finest Italian grand touring cars of its era. The all-steel 2+2 coupÃ© was penned by Giorgetto Giugiaro at Ghia, and combined dramatic proportions with remarkable restraint. 

The Ghibli's low shark-like nose, crisp character lines and muscular fastback profile ran on forged Campagnolo alloy wheels. Sports Car International magazine named it in its top ten Sports Cars of the 1960s.

Named after the hot desert wind of North Africa, the Ghibli was engineered to match its evocative styling. Beneath the long hood was Maserati's 4.7-liter quad-cam V8, featuring dry-sump lubrication and delivering 310 horsepower. 

Offered in period with either the ZF five-speed manual or the Borg-Warner automatic, the rear-wheel drive Ghibli was suited to effortless high-speed touring with refinement befitting the marque. Capable of approximately 155 mph, it ranked among the fastest production automobiles of its day and remains one of Maserati's most celebrated road cars.

THE CAR OFFERED

This car has become known as the 'Playboy Ghibli', as it was gifted to Hefner's girlfriend, Barbi Benton, in 1971 by Hefner himself.

Completed at the Maserati works in September 1967, this Ghibli is a matching-numbers example retaining its original V8 engine and was delivered new to Joseph Massaglia of Santa Monica, California. Factory records confirm its original specification, including Rosso Capannelle over Black Connolly leather, with the desirable Borg-Warner automatic transmission.

Its history soon became intertwined with one of the most recognizable personalities of popular culture. Always a California car, this Maserati was gifted in 1971 to Barbara Klein, better known as Barbi Benton, whose relationship with Hugh Hefner made her one of the defining public figures of the Playboy era. The car remained associated with Playboy Enterprises during the early 1970s and numerous accompanying maintenance invoices issued to both Barbi Benton and Playboy Enterprises provide a fascinating documented record of its careful upkeep during this period. Period photographs and magazine features showing the Ghibli at the Playboy Mansion are also included, with Hugh Hefner and Barbi Benton posing with the Maserati in the background, firmly connecting the car to an iconic moment in American cultural history.

In 1973 ownership transferred to Barbi Benton's father, Dr. Marvin Klein, an obstetrician and gynecologist, before being acquired in 1976 by the present owner. Remaining in the same ownership for nearly five decades, the Ghibli has clearly benefited from long-term stewardship and meticulous care, as well as an extensive restoration, started in 2016 and completed eight years later. As a result, the car took a 3rd place finish in its class at the Concorso Italiano in 2024.

Today, this distinguished Maserati is offered with an extensive portfolio of documents, including the Maserati Certificate of Origin, factory technical specifications, restoration photographs, period magazine articles, historical photographs, ownership records and maintenance receipts spanning much of its life. Combining matching-numbers authenticity, highly desirable factory specifications, documented long-term ownership and celebrity provenance, this early Ghibli represents an exceptional opportunity to acquire one of Maserati's most iconic grand touring automobiles.

1967 Vollstedt-Ford 67 USAC 'Indianapolis' Racing Single-Seater

* Incredibly successful American built race car
* Raced by a roster of legendary drivers
* Shown at the 2018 Pebble Beach Concours and won its class at the 2020 Amelia Island Concours
* A historic piece of motorsports history for show or track

Here, Bonhams is delighted to offer this outstandingly original - and at least equally historic - Indy car built by one of America's most-faithful USAC constructors. 

As expressed in our heading, this Vollstedt-Ford chassis serial '67B' is, not least, the actual car driven by legendary double-Formula 1 World Champion - and 1965 Indianapolis 500-Miles winner - Jim Clark in the 1967 Rex Mays '300' road race at Riverside, California. Regarded at the time (and for many enthusiasts ever since) as one of the greatest racing drivers of all time, international motor racing's humble and gentlemanly Scottish superstar qualified this very car second fastest on the front row of the Riverside starting grid. There, he lined up alongside pole position qualifier Dan Gurney in his Eagle-Ford.

The contemporary Autosport magazine described how: "The moment the pace car pulled off Clark and Gurney streaked away, with the Eagle just in front but with Clark not giving him a moment's peace. After ten laps the rest of the field were strung out behind but still the two Grand Prix boys were hard at it....

"It was Gurney who was in front and under pressure. Eventually he made the slightest mistake and went into a corner too fast, going just wide enough to allow the ever-persistent Clark to sneak through. However, Jimmy's joy was short-lived, for no sooner was the Vollstedt in front than its engine went rough, and he came in to retire with a broken valve."

Very few had expected the Vollstedt to prove as competitive as it had been by its genius driver, and ever-modest Jim Clark later described it as having been "...It's a good motor car - in fact a very good motor car".

The Indy winner and double-World Champion Driver would lose his life the following April in a minor Formula 2 race at Hockenheim, West Germany. That 1967 Rex Mays '300' at Riverside Raceway, and therefore this Vollstedt-Ford '67B' he drove, proved to be Jimmy Clark's last USAC open-wheeler appearance of his glittering career.

But there is more relating to both this car and to Clark. At Riverside this Vollstedt carried a 'surface plate' aerodynamic 'wing' upon its Ford engine's up-raked exhaust system above its tail. Rolla Vollstedt had been amongst the first Indy regulars to recognize the potential of such aerodynamic aids to enhance tire adhesion at exceptionally high speeds. In 1966 he had seen a true airfoil wing adopted on Jerry Eisert's 'Bat Car' entered at Indy by J. Frank Harrison. For this 1967 USAC entry - chassis '67B' now offered here - his plate device sought a similar effect, and it proved sufficiently effective to leave an impression upon its guest driver.

Four months later, Jim Clark was contesting the 1968 Tasman Championship race at Teretonga, New Zealand. His car was a Works-entered Lotus-Cosworth 49T. During practice there he recalled the Vollstedt's 'wing' surface at Riverside and suggested to his mechanics they might try a similar device. Chief mechanic Leo Wybrott and brothers Dale and Roger Porteus had aviation knowledge. They found a discarded helicopter blade in a local scrapyard, sawed off a length and mounted it experimentally on short struts above their Lotus' tail. Leo would recall how Jimmy felt it unwise to race the device after practicing with it, because team chief Colin Chapman was back home in England. If anything went wrong "there would be hell to pay".

But young Ferrari engineer Gianni Marelli photographed the device. Ferrari would arrive for that year's Belgian Grand Prix at high-speed Spa with a strutted wing on their F1 car, as - independently - did the Brabham team. Through 1968 into '69 such strutted wings grew rapidly in size, height, effect and danger until they were banned during the year's Monaco GP meeting. In retrospect, thanks to Jim Clark, that 'winged era' was in part Vollstedt '67B's legacy.

During this historic car's three-year, thirty-race, frontline life it was also driven by two further Indianapolis '500' race winners; Gordon Johncock (victor in 1973 and 1982) and Tom Sneva (1983), among 18 drivers in all. They were - with their major achievements - as follows:

Cale Yarborough (Triple NASCAR Champion, 4-time Daytona '500' Winner, 83 total NASCAR wins)

Carl Williams (Six-time Indy '500' Competitor)

Jim Clark (Twice Formula 1 World Champion, 1965 Indy '500' winner, 2nd 1963 and 1966 Indy '500's)

George Follmer (IndyCar, F1, TransAm, Can-Am, IROC driver, CanAm Champion, TransAm Champion)

Arnie Knepper (USAC driver and five-time Indy 500 competitor)

John Cannon (F5000 Champion, F1 and Indycar driver)

Art Pollard (Seven-time Indy 500 driver, USAC driver)

Larry Dickson (Triple USAC Sprint Car Series Champion, 13-time Indy 500 driver)

Wally Dallenbach (Five-time Indycar winner)

Jim Malloy (Super modified, CAMRA, Indycar driver)

Chris Amon (Formula 1 and Sports car star, McLaren, Ford and Ferrari works driverâwinner of Le Mans and Daytona 24-Hour races)

Gordon Johncock (Twice Indy '500' winner)

Jerry Grant (12 Indy '500's, twice Le Mans 24-Hours competitor, co-driving with Dan Gurney)

Tom Sneva (Indy '500' winner, Super modified and CAMRA driver)

Ronnie Bucknum (Formula 1 and IndyCar competitor)

Tony Adamowicz (sports and TransAm champion)

Denny Zimmerman (IndyCar driver)

Ken Hamilton (Super modified and Sprint Car champion) 

What's more the car qualified for three consecutive Indy 500-Mile races (1967-68-69), and achieved 13 top-ten finishes, three of them in the top five places. And no fewer than four Formula 1 drivers hunkered down into its form-fitting cockpit, including - above all - the late, great Jim Clark...

Canadian-born Rolla Vollstedt - later of Portland, Oregon - was, like so many within the hot-rodder community, an ingenious and thoughtful engineer. He is recalled as having been "passionate, articulate, outspoken and persuasive". He became a high-profile director of the United States Auto Club, and its 1960s-80s car entrant representative.

He had begun building his own race cars in 1955, and aspired to Indy car construction in the early 1960s. He witnessed the advent of rear-engined Formula 1-style cars at Indy when Jack Brabham and Cooper Cars tackled the 1961 '500' - followed by Jim Clark's debutant near win in 1963 with the Lotus-Ford 29. In the Fall of 1963, Rolla Vollstedt brought the first rear-engined Offenhauser-powered car to Indy.

For the 1966 '500' and USAC season, Vollstedt began construction of his first two Lotus-like aluminum monocoque cars. A wooden buck former was finished first by Rolla, John Feuz, and famed fabricator Harold Sperb in Portland, before being used to form the exterior aluminum panels by California Metal Shaping. Two new Vollstedts then followed for 1967, of which '67B' is the second. 

The same wooden buck was used by California Metal Shaping to roll and form the prototype '67 car's outer aluminum monocoque skins. The hull created was some 2 inches wider than '66 form to improve engine access. In Portland, Harold Sperb and John Feuz began building the chassis' complex inner structure, Rolla Vollstedt recording progress in a daily diary. 

He then had '67B's monocoque's skin fabricated by Harold Sperb, himself a local Portland sheet metal specialist. Apart from differing front suspension pickups the two chassis appeared identical. Vollstedt changed his design from Lotus-like inboard front suspension on the '66 cars to Brabham-style outboard on the '67 model.

The engines used were naturally-aspirated fuel-injected 255 cubic-inch (4.2-liter) Ford Racing 4-cam V8s, developing a claimed 500bhp-plus at 8,000rpm. Transmission was via a choice of four-speed Hewland LG500 or two-speed Halibrand gearboxes.

Chassis '67A' was ready for early-season 1967 Firestone tire testing with NASCAR driver Cale Yarborough. Minor misfortune dogged the Vollstedt team at the Indy '500'. During hasty rebuilding of '67A' the two '67 cars' race numbers (17 and 21) were swapped but were stamped on various areas of each car and associated parts. These stamps remain visible today. It was at this time that '67B' became the team's primary car.

After the 500, '67B' finished 10th at Trenton driven by Carl Williams who raced it again at Hanford. It was then in the last USAC race of the year - at Riverside - that Vollstedt ran both his cars; '67A' for Mark Donohue and '67B' for Clark. But when the former's normal entrant Roger Penske heard of his star's plan he vetoed it. 

Rolla Vollstedt told track director Les Richter he was a driver short. Richter suggested that Jim Clark might, perhaps, be available. Jimmy was tracked down vacationing in the Bahamas with his protege Jackie Stewart. A fee of $5,000 was suggested to make the trip to California to drive '67B'. Vollstedt and Richter split the cost 50:50.

The rest is history. And this history in the metal is available right here, right now.

Throughout 1968-69, Vollstedt continued to run the two '67 cars. John Cannon gave the team their best finishes of the year with a second and a sixth in two races at St Jovite/Mt Tremblant, Canada. In the 1969 Indy '500', sprint car champion Larry Dickson then drove '67B' home ninth, Rolla Vollstedt's best finish in the great Indiana classic. 

New driver Dick Simon eventually bought car '67A' while its constructor initially retained '67B' with its Clark history. Within this period, '67B' became a Hollywood star, featuring in the Paul Newman/Joanne Woodward/Robert Wagner movie Winning. Turbocharged variants of the 4-cam Ford V8s and stock-block Chevrolet engines were tried in place of the obsolescent original normally-aspirated 4-cam Ford V8s, but eventually a new McLaren was acquired and Vollstedt's ageing '67 car relegated to team spare. 

Late in 1972, Vollstedt sold it to fellow Oregonian and long-time sprint car owner Art Sugai for his driver Kenny Hamilton. They had Rolla and his team lengthen the wheelbase 6 inches but in practice at Phoenix, Hamilton crashed, damaging the left-side tub and suspensions. The car never raced again. 

Sugai later acquired the ex-Simon sister car '67A'. It was sold to Australian collector Peter Briggs in July 1980 and displayed in his York Motor Museum as 'the Clark Vollstedt'. When offered by BONHAMS at the 2009 Quail Lodge Auction in Monterey, California, its correct identity was quickly established and correction made. 

Meanwhile Sugai's chief mechanic, Tom Fox, had acquired '67B' and many related parts, including its original wooden panel-forming buck. The car passed to Fox's friend Ron Yurich, who planned to rebuild it as a super modified sprint car. But '67B' then lay half-forgotten for nearly 20 years in storage. Following Yurich's passing in 2006, his son John finally offered '67B' for sale. Kurt Vollstedt eventually mentioned the car's re-emergence to the current owner, who then found the car and parts stacked in a dilapidated wooden former machine shop in Silverdale, Washington, its tub exactly as immediately after Hamilton's Phoenix crash. Many parts were available. Even the body buck was there. 

This piece of history was duly acquired by the current owner and back in the Pacific north-west painstaking restoration began. 

Most notably, all original parts and even many minor 'battle scars' were located, retained or preserved (such as new old-stock cast-magnesium suspension uprights). Importantly, the owner succeeded (amazingly) in rediscovering the car's original Riverside 'wing', still bearing the legend Clark's personal autograph and its period decal. 

Such a survivor as this Vollstedt is exceedingly rare automotive archaeology. It speaks to us. An as-original engine, and gearbox parts, had to be sourced - and they were duly obtained eventually from none other than four-time Indy '500' winner (1970-71-78-87) and former Jim Clark team-mate, Al Unser...

Post-restoration the car has only been presented publicly in the most exclusive prestige events. It was invited to attend the 2017 Goodwood Festival of Speed, and then to take its place at the 2018 Pebble Beach Concours as one of the most significant Indy cars of the 1960s. It also became a class winner at the 2020 Amelia Island Concours. 

We at Bonhams heartily recommend the closest possible consideration of this remarkable race car. Vollstedt-Ford '67B' offered here has rare appeal. It is truly historic, an archaeological piece. It breathes originality and - subject to adequate inspection - it is on the button - ready to run. One decisive bid - it really can be your's.

THE ALFA ROMEO GIULIA 

When Alfa Romeo resolved to take Bertone's elegant 105-Series coupe racing, the task fell to Autodelta, the firm's competition department under Carlo Chiti. The result was the GTA â the 'A' standing for Alleggerita, or lightened â its steel outer panels exchanged for Peraluman 25 aluminum alloy, shedding some 200 kilograms from the standard Sprint GT. Beneath the lightweight skin came a twin-plug cylinder head, enlarged valves, 45mm Weber carburetors, raised compression, and magnesium castings for the cam cover, sump, and timing cover. For circuit work, Autodelta offered its ingenious 'sliding block' rear axle location, transforming the car's handling. 

The GTA claimed the European Touring Car Championship in 1966, 1967, and 1969, and SCCA B Sedan titles in America in 1966 and 1970 with Horst Kwech. As competition intensified in the 1300cc class in Europe and C Sedan in America, Alfa Romeo introduced the GTA 1300 Junior for 1968, a short-stroke 1,290cc derivative that went on to win the European Touring Car Championship in 1971 and 1972 and the SCCA C Sedan national championship in 1969 and 1971. An Alfa led the 1970 run offs until an unfortunate DNF elevated a Mini to the win. Of the approximately 450 GTA 1300 Juniors built for homologation, the great majority were finished in Stradale trim; genuine Autodelta-prepared Corsa examples are rare and highly prized today.

THE CAR OFFERED

Built in 1968 and prepared by Autodelta to full Corsa specification, chassis 775511 was placed by Alfa Romeo's competition director Don Black to its first owner, Eugene Strandberg of Des Moines, Iowa, the sale having been brokered through New Jersey dealer Tom O'Brien as Alfa Romeo itself could not sell directly to customers. While Autodelta's own records on GTA Juniors to the US do not survive, the car's competition provenance is firmly established by two independent sources within the history file: period correspondence with Strandberg, and a hand-written note from Don Black himself, dated 1992, confirming that 775511 was one of the first five Autodelta-prepared GTA Juniors imported into the United States by Alfa Romeo. Black's testimony carries particular weight, as Alfa Romeo's longtime Technical Director in North America from the 1960s through the 1990s and the man who managed the marque's U.S. competition programs and Alfa Corse operations. These first five cars were specifically sold to owners who would take them racing and promote Alfa's on track success in the C Sedan category.

What followed was a twelve-year American racing career. Original SCCA logbooks, photographs, and correspondence with all six owner-drivers document more than 50 SCCA-sanctioned meetings between 1968 and 1980 at circuits including Road America, Road Atlanta, Daytona, Indianapolis, and Bridgehampton. 

The car qualified three times for the SCCA National Runoffs, with Strandberg finishing 10th at Daytona in 1969, Bob Henson 4th at Road Atlanta in 1971, and Jerry Wannarka, later SCCA Chairman, 7th at Road Atlanta in 1974. Dismantled after its final race in 1980 in anticipation of a restoration that never came, 775511 remained in that state for 35 years until acquired by the current owner in 2015 and shipped to Australia, where it received a five-year restoration by Alfa specialists Tim Doyle of Zoo Autocraft, Mick Mitchell of Corse Automotive Services, and Vin Sharp of Pace Engineering, at a cost exceeding AU$400,000.

The car retains its original bodyshell, with 775511 stamped on the bulkhead, and its original matching-numbers engine block (01068), which accompanies the car. To preserve that block, a new engine was built upon an original, unused, and unnumbered 1300 block supplied with the car, producing approximately 135bhp at 7,700rpm. Highlights of the restoration include correct DCOE18 Weber 45 carburetors with original hand-finished intake trumpets, correct magnesium head and sump castings, a close-ratio gearbox built by Pace Engineering to correct original GTA ratios, the original restored Autodelta-stamped sliding block, original Veglia instruments, the correct S132 Magneti Marelli distributor case fitted with electronic ignition and an FIA-approved welded-in safety cage from Alfaholics UK. The car is finished in its original colour of Biancospino, "hawthorn white", with contrasting green side stripes, Alfa Romeo logos, and number 48 racing roundels on the doors and hood, presented in the livery in which it first raced, over a largely stripped-out black vinyl and interior accented by the orginal dash and chrome trim. Further period-correct equipment includes plexiglass side and rear windows, Facet fuel pumps, a period-style external fuel filler, a wood-rimmed Hellebore steering wheel, a Schroth Racing driver's harness, a driver's bucket seat, and replica Carello headlights, with 14-inch replica Campagnolo-style alloy wheels in gunmetal grey fitted with Dunlop Racing tires. Two ignition keys accompany the car.

Since restoration, 775511 has been enjoyed on several track outings at Philip Island, Australia. Holding a Motorsport Australia Group T logbook, it has also been campaigned at Wakefield Park and Sydney Motorsport Park. At Auto Italia, Australia's premier Italian classic car show, it won the sponsor's Perpetual Trophy in 2021 and returned in 2022 to be voted Best Alfa Romeo and People's Choice for Best Car, standing as one of four Best of Show finalists from a field of 350. It placed 2nd in two concours categories at Motorclassica in 2022 and was among just 40 cars invited to the Sydney Harbour Concours d'Elegance in 2024. The car has only been raced sparingly â twice at Wakefield Park (2021 and 2022), three times at Sydney Motorsport Park (2023 and 2024) and once at Phillip Island (2025). Documented by Martin Ãbelher, author of Alleggerita, the definitive GTA reference, and offered with its original SCCA logbooks, correspondence with previous owners, period photographs, and original numbered engine block, chassis 775511 presents a nearly unrepeatable opportunity to buy a historic and fully documented Alfa Romeo GTA 1300 Junior Corsa.

THE ALFA ROMEO 2000 SPIDER

In 1958, Alfa came out with a new sedan, which, with its larger 1,975cc engine, was called the 2000. There was, not surprisingly, a 2000 Spider, designed and built by Touring, and a 2000 Sprint Coupe done by Bertone, the latter introduced in 1960. Spider and Sprint production comprised nearly half of all 2000 salesâ3,443 examples of the Spider were produced, and 700 of the more expensive Sprint Coupe. The 2000 sedan had the uncommon feature of a column-mounted shifter for its five-speed transmission, while the Spider and Sprint retained the more sporting-oriented floor-mounted gear shift.

Built between 1958 and 1962, the 2000 Spider was far rarer than its junior counterpart, the Giulietta Spider (of which about 17,000 were produced), and at $5,365 POE, its price was much greater than that of the smaller car. The 1975cc 4-Cylinder engine, with duplex-chain driven twin overhead camshafts, hemispherical combustion chambers, and a pair of side-draft Solex carburetors, was tuned to deliver 131 horsepower, allowing the Touring-bodied roadster to easily exceed 100 mph. Its fully-synchronized 5-Speed transmission allowed fairly relaxed high-speed touring, and its large Alfin drum brakes were extremely effective for their day. The handsome unibody styled by Carrozzeria Touring on a 98-inch wheelbase presaged what would become the six-cylinder 2600 convertible in 1962.

The first known history of the car documents that it was a largely original and unrestored car when it was sold in Indiana in September of 1998. Restored a few years later in California, it would remain in California for much of the next two decades. Acquired by the current owner eight years ago, the now quarter of a century old restoration has mellowed nicely with age.

This rare, top-of-the-line 2000 Touring is eligible for exclusive driving events around the globe and will surely provide its driver with many smile-inducing experiences. A fine example of open top motoring with excellent road holding and high-revving twin-cam performance, the 2000 Spider rightly claims its place in the Alfa lineage.

THE MERCEDES-BENZ 300 S

Introduced at the Paris Salon in October 1951, the Mercedes-Benz 300 S represented the pinnacle of the Stuttgart manufacturer's post-war production. Built entirely by hand and offered in CoupÃ©, Cabriolet and Roadster forms, the W188 combined refined luxury with advanced engineering at a level unmatched by virtually any contemporary European automobile. Costing approximately fifty percent more than the already prestigious 300 "Adenauer" saloon, the 300 S was intended for an exclusive clientele seeking effortless performance, impeccable craftsmanship and understated elegance.

Production remained intentionally limited. Between 1952 and 1955 just 560 examples of the 300 S were completed across all body styles, including only 216 fixed-head CoupÃ©s. Their rarity, craftsmanship and close relationship to Mercedes-Benz's most important post-war models have established the 300 S as one of the marque's most desirable luxury automobiles. Today they remain highly prized by collectors for their elegance, exclusivity and engineering.

THE CAR OFFERED

Believed to have remained in Europe during its early life, this 1953 Mercedes-Benz 300 S is accompanied by documentation that provides a fascinating glimpse into its first years of ownership. Surviving workshop invoices record maintenance and repairs performed in Hamburg, Hannover and Nuremberg through 1959. One repair record from April of that year notes the odometer at 86,387 kilometers, confirming that the car was actively enjoyed on German roads before eventually making its way to the United States.

The Mercedes found a new home in America on 13 May 1963 when it was acquired on Mercer Island, Washington, by Dr. Wallace Nelson. Dr. Nelson's life was as remarkable as the automobiles he collected. Born to Swedish immigrant parents during the Roaring Twenties and raised throughout the Great Depression, he served during the Second World War with the 98th Bomb Group of the United States Army Air Corps. Following the war, he pursued a distinguished medical career, serving aboard the United States Coast Guard icebreaker Northwind before becoming a neurological specialist in Washington State and later consulting for the government of Singapore.

Despite his demanding profession, Dr. Nelson nurtured a lifelong enthusiasm for distinguished automobiles. Family members fondly recall his spontaneous approach to collecting, often leaving home in one vehicle only to return later that day having traded it for another. His acquisition of this Mercedes-Benz perfectly illustrates that passion.

Family records, including his wife's diary, preserve the story of the day the Mercedes entered the Nelson household. On 13 May 1963, Dr. Nelson left home driving an Oldsmobile convertible and returned instead with the elegant German CoupÃ©. After taking his wife and one of her friends for a celebratory drive, he reportedly declared the Mercedes "too special to drive." True to his word, the car was carefully garaged shortly thereafter, beginning an extraordinary period of preservation spanning more than six decades.

Stored since 1964, the Mercedes survives today as an unusually untouched example of one of Stuttgart's rarest post-war grand tourers. Although the odometer presently displays 1,644 kilometers, period workshop documentation confirms that it has rolled over, suggesting its actual reading should be approximately 101,644 kilometers (63,159 miles), entirely consistent with its documented European use.

The accompanying records also reveal that the car was originally finished in an elegant green with matching green interior trim before being refinished in silver during its lifetime. Replacement fuel tank and fuel hoses have been fitted, although these components are acknowledged as later service replacements rather than original factory equipment.

This car emerges unique not only for its rarity but the authenticity of its story. Having been preserved for more than sixty years by one family and accompanied by period documentation spanning both Europe and America, marks this 300 S as a rare find. The combination of documented European history, ownership by a distinguished physician and veteran, and decades of careful storage creates a compelling provenance.

Whether carefully recommissioned for concours exhibition, sympathetic preservation, or inclusion within a significant Mercedes-Benz collection, this exceptionally rare 300 S CoupÃ© represents an increasingly elusive opportunity. One of only 216 CoupÃ©s produced, it embodies the craftsmanship, engineering excellence and restrained elegance that defined Mercedes-Benz at the dawn of the post-war era and remains among the marque's finest grand touring automobiles.

Mercedes-Benz unveiled its first new post-war flagship sedan at the Frankfurt Auto Show in 1951. The elegant 300 sedan was an imposing statement of European luxury, offered as either a four-door sedan or four-door full convertible. The press and buying public praised it for its exceptional engineering and build quality, and it soon became a favorite among celebrities and heads of state alike, including Chancellor Konrad Adenauer, whose affinity for the sedan earned it the eponymous nickname.

Mercedes-Benz followed with a more sporting version, the 300Sâthe "S" denoting it as Super. The 300S chassis was shortened by 25 centimeters and offered as an elegant coupe, glamorous open-topped cabriolet, or a disappearing-top roadster, all built at the renowned Sindelfingen factory. In essence, the 300S was the post-war spiritual successor to the legendary 540K. The S-specification cars featured an uprated 3.0-liter inline-six with 3 Solex carburetors and a boosted compression ratio to make 150bhp, up from the standard car's 115bhp. The engine is backed by a smooth and reliable four-speed manual with a delightfully slick column shift. The suspension is independent in front with a swing axle arrangement in the rear, sprung with coils. While tuned for comfort, the 300S is still a respectable handler and is impressively poised at speed. The solid road feel and opulent appointments made the 300S a very special place to spend time.

Exclusivity was assured as only 560 examples of the 300S were hand-built between 1952 and 1958. That exclusivity also came with a price: A whopping $12,680 in 1953âabout twice the price of a new Cadillac. Notable 300S owners included Cary Grant, Gary Cooper, and The Aga Khan, who all could easily afford the cost of entry into this limited club.

A wonderful example of fastidious preservation, this marvelous 300S Cabriolet has survived unrestored for nearly seventy years save one respray in its original Graphite Grey color. Factory production records on file show this car was delivered to the USA on December 18, 1954, via Mercedes-Benz of New York. A richly appointed red leather interior and black canvas top round the aesthetic, which surely made a dramatic statement rolling on to the boulevard in 1955. The car's early ownership history is not currently known, however, in 1974 it was acquired by the most recent owners from the noted marque specialist Alex Dearborn. At the time, it was a completely original, untouched car and thankfully, the new custodians recognized its value and strove to maintain its originality. In 1986, it received a lacquer repaint in its factory color, which it still wears today. The interior is a particular highlight, displaying a fabulous patina on the red leather seats and panels. Expansive woodwork and chrome switchgear add to the opulent feel, and the car retains authentic details including the original Becker radio and factory parts manual.

The 300S is renowned for its superb build quality, which is undoubtedly a factor in this car's impressive survival. It benefits from recent servicing, and the consignor reports it to be fine runner. Additionally, it retains its numbers-matching six-cylinder engine which is tidy, honest, and consistent with the unrestored quality. With its rich patina and appealing authenticity this car will undoubtedly show well in concours preservation classes.

After seven decades of attentive care, this rare and highly desirable Mercedes-Benz 300S is once again ready for a new custodian to usher it into its next chapter.

* VARA B Production Champion in 1992, 1993, and 1994 with 19 race victories
* Monterey Historics veteran and regarded as one of the most successful vintage racing Jaguars in America
* Later owned by actor Nicolas Cage and registered for road use

THE JAGUAR XKE

When the XKE debuted in 1961, it was an instant hit. The aerodynamic design was not just a pretty faÃ§ade, as the indomitable XKE lived up to its good looks by clocking top speeds in excess of 150 miles an hour. The E-Type was the fastest production car of its era. Not only beautiful and fast, the car was reasonably priced and became Britain's favorite motoring sports car and a racing celebrity.

THE CAR OFFERED

Among Jaguar competition cars active in American vintage racing during the late twentieth century, few achieved the reputation, success, and recognition of E-Type No. 46. For more than a decade, this distinctive green coupe dominated West Coast vintage racing grids under the stewardship of Swiss-born Jaguar specialist Bernard Juchli, who went on to become the general manager of Jay Leno's Big Dog Garage in Burbank, California. Under Juchli's stewardship, No. 46 earned multiple championships, becoming a fixture at the Monterey Historics, and establishing itself as one of the most successful and recognizable E-Types in the country.

No. 46 began life as a 1963 Jaguar E-Type Fixed Head Coupe before entering competition use early in its career. By the time it was acquired by Bernard Juchli and his partner at Jaguars Unlimited, the car was already a seasoned race car. Although worn and in need of comprehensive restoration, it retained many of the key features that hinted at its competitive past, including an aluminum hood, Weber carburetors, a dry-sump lubrication system, suspension modifications, and a roll cage.

Rather than restoring the Jaguar to road-going specification, Juchli envisioned something altogether different: a purpose-built vintage racing E-Type capable of winning at the highest levels of competition while maintaining the reliability necessary to complete full racing seasons.

The car was stripped completely to its bare shell, revealing extensive corrosion throughout the lower structure. The floor sections were beyond repair, and the body required significant reconstruction. The shell was mounted upside down, the deteriorated floor removed entirely, and an integrated eight-point roll cage fabricated before new structural panels were installed. Juchli personally carried out much of the work, utilizing the facilities of Jaguars Unlimited to create what would become one of the most developed and successful vintage racing Jaguars of its era.

Lightweight construction became a central theme of the build. Aluminum doors and rear hatch panels were fabricated, Lexan windows installed throughout, and the rain gutters eliminated entirely to improve aerodynamics. A specially configured windshield extending farther forward than the standard E-Type design improved airflow over the roof. Completed, the car weighed approximately 2,340 pounds, substantially lighter than a standard production E-Type.

Mechanically, No. 46 evolved continuously throughout its competition career. Utilizing the 3.8-liter engine, which produced approximately 365 horsepower at 6,500 rpm on the dynamometer and approached 400 horsepower under ideal conditions, Juchli retained Jaguar's legendary twin-cam inline-six architecture, with virtually every component optimized for racing use. Only the basic block, head casting, and crankshaft remained fundamentally Jaguar. The dry-sump system was rebuilt and refined, cooling was upgraded with lightweight aluminum components, and extensive development produced an engine that combined exceptional performance with remarkable durability. Unlike many highly tuned competition engines that required constant rebuilding, Juchli's race motors were engineered for longevity and reliability, a philosophy that would prove critical to the car's success.

The transmission received similar attention. A close-ratio gearbox was fitted with specially designed racing synchronizers developed by Juchli after repeated failures of conventional components. Combined with a Tilton aluminum flywheel and triple-plate clutch, the result was a drivetrain capable of handling the engine's increased output while remaining dependable throughout a demanding racing schedule. In Juchli's own words, the car received thousands of hours of work and thousands of dollar's worth of upgrades. The result is priceless.

By the early 1990s, No. 46 had become the benchmark Jaguar in West Coast vintage racing competition. Under Juchli's ownership and driving, the E-Type captured VARA B Production Championships in 1992, 1993, and 1994 while accumulating an extraordinary nineteen race victories.

Its dominance became so pronounced that the Jaguar was moved from C Production, where it naturally belonged, into the more competitive B Production category. There it faced formidable opposition from Shelby Cobras and V8-powered Corvettes yet continued to deliver winning performances. According to Juchli, the car recorded no race retirements during its final two seasons of active competition under his ownershipâan extraordinary achievement for a front-running vintage race car. The Jaguar became a familiar and respected presence at the Monterey Historic Automobile Races, where it competed successfully for more than ten years. During this period, No. 46 developed a reputation as the car to beat and earned recognition among competitors and spectators alike as 'the winningest vintage racing Jag in the West'!

Following its championship-winning career, the E-Type entered private ownership and later passed to actor Nicolas Cage. Cage reportedly registered the car for street use and used it while preparing for the driving sequences featured in the film Gone in 60 Seconds. While many former race cars lose their identity following retirement from competition, No. 46 retained the character and presence that had made it famous on the track.

Today, No. 46 represents a rare opportunity to acquire a Jaguar competition car whose significance derives from decades of documented achievement. Developed by one of America's most respected Jaguar specialists, campaigned to multiple championships, and remembered by generations of vintage racers as the dominant E-Type of its era, it occupies a unique place in the history of American vintage motorsport. For collectors seeking a proven and celebrated competition Jaguar, few E-Types can match the combination of pedigree and performance embodied by the legendary No. 46. Add to that the Jaguar's celebrity ownership with Nicholas Cage and its role in his preparation for one of the most iconic motoring films of modern times, and the legendary No. 46 is itself a celebrity not to be overlooked.

THE FERRARI DINO 246 GT

A 2.4-liter version on a longer wheelbase - the 246 GT - replaced the original Dino 206 in late 1969. Built by Scaglietti, the body was now steel, and the cylinder block cast-iron rather than aluminum, but the bigger engine's increased power - 195bhp at 7,600rpm - adequately compensated for the weight gain. A Targa-top version, the 246 GTS, followed in 1972. The Dino 246 was built in three series: 'L', 'M' and 'E', these designations reflecting detail changes in the specification. Of the three, the M-series is by far the rarest, being produced during the early months of 1971 only. Changes from the preceding L-series included a 30mm increase in rear track; five-bolt fixing for the road wheels; internal trunk release; seat-mounted headrests; and various minor improvements to the engine and gearbox. The final 'E' series incorporated all the changes made to its predecessors together with further improvements to the engine and gearbox and numerous other more minor details. 

While not quite as fast in a straight line as its larger V12-engined stablemates, the nimble Dino was capable of showing almost anything a clean pair of heels over twisty going. Truly a driver's car par excellence and still highly regarded today.

THE CAR OFFERED

Completed on November 10, 1972, chassis 04382 was delivered new in the timeless and highly desirable color combination of Rosso Chiaro over Pelle Beige, a specification it proudly retains today. Imported to the United States through William F. Harrah's renowned Ferrari distributorship, Modern Classic Motors of Reno, Nevada, the Dino was subsequently supplied to Steve Griswold & Co. of Berkeley, California. Its first owner, Page Roos of San Mateo, California would enjoy long-term stewardship of the car for well over a decade, establishing an early history of careful ownership.

According to the accompanying Marcel Massini Report, the Dino remained registered in California for nearly half a century before relocating to Canada in 2021. That same year, its prior owner embarked upon an extensive mechanical restoration performed by Ferrari Classiche-certified technicians, with expenditures approaching $80,000. The work included replacement of key mechanical and electrical components, including the shifter assembly, wiring, radiator, blower motors, thermostat, and numerous gaskets, while cosmetic refinements encompassed restored chrome trim, refinished brake calipers, underbody detailing, and new tires. Most importantly, this meticulous attention to originality and authenticity culminated in the car earning Ferrari Classiche Certification in January 2023.

Acquired by the current owner in March of 2024, it has been driven sparingly but received an extensive, engine out service and detailing that was only completed weeks before the auction. Five pages of detailed invoices layout the work completed including removing the drivetrain, rebuilding the transmission, replacement of gaskets and seals in both the engine and transmission, rebuilding the carburetors, replacing hoses, engine tune up, brake and coolant system flushes, deep cleaning of the engine bay and drivetrain componentry, and more. Following the extensive rebuild, service, and tune-up, the car received a thorough paint correction and detailing. The invoices for work completed total over $64,000.

Accompanying the Dino are its coveted Classiche Red Book, badge, and libretto, confirming its conformity to factory specifications. Retaining its matching-numbers engine and transmission, chassis 04382 is additionally offered with its original owner's manuals, warranty card, and tool kit. Beautifully preserved in its original color scheme and recognized by Ferrari's most rigorous certification program, this exceptional Dino 246 GT presents a compelling opportunity to acquire one of Maranello's most celebrated and enduring designsâequally suited to concours presentation, touring events, or spirited enjoyment on the open road.

THE FERRARI 365 GTC/4

Introduced at the March 1971 Geneva Motor Show, the Ferrari 365 GTC/4 was derived from the chassis of the 365GTB/4 Daytona of 1968. The engine was similar to the 4,390cc DOHC V12 of the Daytona, but new heads and a lower compression ratio of 8.8:1 lowered the brake horsepower to 340, slightly less for emissions-controlled American cars. Six side-draft Weber 38 DCOE carburetors fueled the engine, which used wet sump lubrication.

The wheelbase, at 94.5 inches, remained unchanged. Improvements included standard power steering and a larger luggage compartment, while the side-draft carburetors allowed a lower hood line. In contrast to the Daytona, however, which used a rear-mounted transaxle, the GTC/4 had its gearbox, a five-speed manual unit, mounted to the engine. The suspension was independent all around, with unequal-length control arms and coil springs, an anti-roll bar and hydraulic self-leveling.

Designed and built by Pininfarina, the coupe bodies were shipped to Maranello for assembly. The low hood permitted by the side-draft carburetors incorporated retractable headlamps, and a handsome Kamm tail featured traditional Ferrari tail lamps. The interior was a completely new design with more comfortable seating, although the occasional "+2" seats in the rear were best used folded as luggage space. The seats had cloth inserts as standard, for comfort in warm weather, although air conditioning was standard. Full leather upholstery was available as an option.

The 365 GTC/4's handling has always been described as "phenomenal," even when taking into consideration the tire technology of the time. The brakes, combined with the 11-plus-inch ventilated discs all around, were similarly up to the task.

Just 505 GTC/4s were built from 1971 to 1973. Road & Track called the GTC/4 "a graceful, clean and understated design"; it is all of that and more.

THE CAR OFFERED

Completed in June 1972, this U.S.-delivery Ferrari 365 GTC/4 was supplied new through the renowned Chinetti-Garthwaite Ferrari dealership in Pennsylvania. Research by respected Ferrari historian Marcel Massini confirms that its first owner was Rodolfo Junco de la Vega, Jr., a prominent newspaper publisher based in San Antonio, Texas. A dedicated Ferrari enthusiast, Mr. de la Vega cherished the GTC/4 for nearly five decades, maintaining continuous ownership until his passing in October 2020. The car was then sold in 2022 moving to Florida, then again changed hands in 2024 where it has spent time exploring the Midwest. 

With just under 32,000 miles, this wonderful GT car is a testament to the maintenance and care it received from its long-term owner. Cosmetically, the cars original livery was changed to the quite attractive hue of Blu Ahrabian paintwork, presenting with an impressive luster. The interior appears to be largely original, finished in its original color of Beige. This GTC/4 has been very well maintained in its current ownership. The car includes some of its recent service records including a receipt for its most recent major service, performed by a marque expert at the end of 2024 at a total cost of over $72,000.

Overall, this is a very fine and attractive example of a 2+2 Ferrari, with most of its history known. It is also low-mileage and highly cared for throughout the years. Few 2+2 Ferraris are as exciting and desirable as the C4, thanks to their rarity, low-slung hood, elegant roofline and drivability. 

Included in the sale of this great Ferrari are the books, some receipts as well as the Marcel Massini history report. Surely a wonderful example to experience front-engined V12 prowess from Maranello.

THE 550 MARANELLO

With the introduction of the 550 Maranello in 1997, Ferrari returned to its tradition of building front-engined V12 sports cars, resurrecting a line that had remained dormant since the demise of the 365GTB/4 'Daytona' in 1974. The heart of any Ferrari is its engine, and the 550 Maranello's 48-valve, 5.5-liter V12 developed 485bhp at 7,000rpm, some 100-or-so horsepower more than the Daytona's. Ferrari had discovered long ago that providing optimum balance in a front-engined sports car necessitated the use of a rear transaxle, and the Maranello's came with six speeds. The power train was housed in a tubular steel chassis, to which was attached aluminum coachwork, while the all-independent suspension incorporated dual-mode (normal/sports) damping, switch-selectable by the driver, which was complemented by speed-sensitive power-assisted steering.

Styled by Pininfarina like its illustrious 'Daytona' predecessor, the 550 Maranello was similarly proportioned, adopting the classical combination of long hood, small cabin and truncated tail. The body's aerodynamics were developed in the wind tunnel, where hours of testing ensured that the minimum of drag was combined with constant downforce regardless of set up, an important consideration in a 200mph road car. Styling details such as the hood air scoop and hot air outlets behind the front wheelarches recalled the great competizione Ferraris of the past, in particular the immortal 250GTO, while the tail incorporated Ferrari's characteristic twin circular lights.

In 2004, Evo magazine published a 'Greatest Driver's Cars' feature that pitted the 550 Maranello against the Porsche 911 GT3, Honda NSX-R and Pagani Zonda C12S. The Ferrari won. "As with all great cars, there's no one facet that dominates the experience," declared the respected British motoring journal. "Yes, the engine is mighty, but the chassis is its equal. There's never been a supercar that's so exploitable and so rounded in its capabilities."

THE CAR OFFERED

This sublimely elegant and understated 550 Maranello, was commissioned in the classic scheme of Rosso Corsa over black leather. The Ferrari was delivered to its first owner in France on January 16, 1998, and spend the first eight years and 7,900 kilometers of its life in scenic France. From about 2013 until 2015 the sleek coupe blitzed about the green roads of Switzerland. Following its brief Swiss ownership, the car made the trek over to the UK around 2016 until about 2024 before making the long journey over to the United States. 

The car has received regular maintenance throughout its life, as evidenced by the service booklet showing consistent servicing despite the very low mileage. This 550M will be accompanied by many of its recent service invoices. The current mileage at the time of photography shows just under 14,300 kilometers (8,885 miles). The last service was performed in July 2024 where it received new cambelts. Cosmetically, the interior and exterior are very well presented and detailed. 

Showing very much as it left the factory, save for the low mileage and just a touch of wear, the only addition is the upgraded stereo head unit in the dash. This fantastic GT Ferrari, with its front mounted V12 full of torque, continues to be one of the greatest modern touring cars to come out of Maranello, so fitting as they named this legendary car after the city it was assembled in. 

A great car to enjoy, this spiritual successor to the legendary Daytona is swiftly becoming an icon in its own right and would make a welcome addition to any garage!
