THE PROTOTYPE TECHNOLOGY GROUP

Prototype Technology Group (PTG Racing Inc.), run by Tom Milner of Winchester Virginia, was contracted by BMW of North America from 1995 through 2006, to serve as BMW's North American research and development racing team, which campaigned the BMW M3 in the racing series of IMSA, USRC, ALMS, SCCA World Challenge as well as Grand-AM.

Milner was a German-born engineer who immigrated to the US and spent decades building one of the most respected sports car programs in the country. He had over 30 years of experience across IMSA, SCCA, and NASCAR, with early accomplishments including a partnership with Bill Scott Racing that produced 10 championships in Formula Vee, Super Vee, and Formula Ford from 1967 to 1984.

He set up on his own in 1988 as Tom Milner Racing, then changed the team's name to PTG ahead of the BMW program â he arrived at the name by reversing the letters of IMSA's GTP class. 

PTG represented BMW North America's factory-backed sports car racing effort in much the same way that Pratt & Miller came to define Corvette Racing. Between 1995 and 2006, the team amassed an extraordinary 53 victories from 118 starts while securing 14 championships across IMSA, USRRC, ALMS, and Grand-Am competition. The E46 M3 GT program represented the pinnacle of that partnership. Introduced for the 2000 season, the cars immediately emerged as formidable contenders in the fiercely competitive GT category, taking the fight directly to the dominant Porsche 911 GT3-R on circuits throughout North America and Europe.

Championships included four sports-car manufacturer titles for BMW, four team titles, and three driver championships. 

The team closed its doors in 2013. Tom's son Tommy Milner went on to become a factory Corvette/BMW endurance driver in his own right â a true racing family legacy.

THE CAR OFFERED

Among the most significant BMW competition cars ever constructed in North America, BMW Motorsport E46 GT chassis 00/001 is far more than the first example of its typeâit is the very chassis from which the entire E46 M3 racing program was developed. Constructed by Tom Milner's Prototype Technology Group (PTG) at the direction of BMW of North America, this development car preceded every subsequent E46 GT and served as the benchmark against which the remainder of the program would be measured.

Chassis 00/001 was entrusted to three of the era's most respected names in GT racing. Le Mans legend and longtime BMW factory driver Hans-Joachim Stuck shared driving duties with the immensely talented Boris Said and future ALMS GT standout Johannes van Overbeek. Together, they campaigned this chassis at Sebring, Charlotte, Silverstone, and the NÃ¼rburgring, giving the car an international competition history of genuine significance.

Following its tenure with PTG, the car was sold to Alegra Motorsport, where it continued its professional racing life in Grand-Am competition. In endurance trim, it competed in some of North America's premier events, including the Rolex 24 At Daytona, the 12 Hours of Sebring, and the Six Hours of The Glen before eventually retiring from frontline competition and briefly appearing in Historic Sportscar Racing events. During this period, the car underwent numerous livery changes and modifications to comply with evolving regulations, obscuring its identity as the original PTG development chassis.

That changed in 2009 when the late David Paul of Allentown, Pennsylvaniaâa close friend of noted BMW racer and constructor David Mooreâset out to acquire a PTG BMW for HSR competition. During a pre-purchase inspection at David Hinton's workshop in Tampa, Florida, Moore made an extraordinary discovery: the car under consideration was none other than chassis 00/001 itself, the original PTG E46 development car.

The discovery prompted a decision that went far beyond conventional race preparation. Rather than preparing the BMW for contemporary historic competition, the new custodians committed to a painstaking restoration to its original ALMS specification and livery. The sole deviation from factory configuration was the retention of the enlarged 3.4-liter engine, developed by PTG's Chris Fletcher from the original 3.2-liter unit to enhance competitiveness during the car's later career.

To ensure complete accuracy, Moore enlisted Scott Clarke, the car's original crew chief during its ALMS campaigns, to advise on the distinctions between its original configuration and subsequent Grand-Am modifications. The restoration became something of an archaeological exercise, revealing that the car remarkably retained its original bodywork, engine, gearbox, drivetrain, suspension, and numerous other components from its period competition life. Most notably, it still possessed the unique rear "M" firewall exclusive to chassis 00/001, a feature never carried over to later examples.

Every detail was recreated from original drawings and period photography. The ALMS-specification aero exits in the front fenders, filled during the Grand-Am years, were reopened to reveal the original carbon-fiber structure beneath. The lightweight PTG door frames and Lexan glazing were restored, while the distinctive angled M5-derived radiator and bespoke intake ducting were faithfully reinstated. Moore also enlisted renowned IMSA and ALMS photographer Bruce Miller, whose extensive archive of period imagery proved invaluable in documenting the car's original appearance. Ultimately, the restoration team chose to return the BMW to the livery it carried during the 2000 Bitburger/AvD 1000 Kilometer NÃ¼rburgring race in the Le Mans Series.

Upon completion, chassis 00/001 made a fitting public return when it was displayed at The Quail in 2009 as part of the Hans Stuck Tribute, honoring one of the men most closely associated with its early career.

Today, the car is presented in that same NÃ¼rburgring specification and livery, accompanied by comprehensive documentation supporting its identity and provenance. No other BMW E46 M3 GT occupies the position this chassis holds in the history of BMW motorsport in North America. It is the first of the lineâthe development car that established the standard for every E46 GT that followedâand survives today as one of the most important and carefully preserved artifacts of BMW's modern American racing history.

THE CAR OFFERED

Conceived as a technological showcase and design statement, this remarkable one-off BMW 635 CSi stands among the most intriguing British coachbuilt projects of the 1980s. Internally designated "Special Project M3" by Coventry-based MGA Developments Ltd., the car was created to demonstrate the company's full spectrum of engineering, styling, and prototype-development capabilities. Established in 1979 by Mike Gibbs, MGA provided design-to-production services for major automotive manufacturers, and this ambitious project served as its ultimate calling card.

Supplied new by BMW Great Britain in 1982 and financially supported by The Observer newspaper, the donor 635 CSi was transformed into what was envisioned as the world's first fully retractable glass-roofed grand tourer. Developed in conjunction with Triplex Safety Glass and Tudor sunroof mechanisms, the innovative roof system employed a sophisticated arrangement whereby multiple glass panels and the rear window retracted into a specially engineered compartment within the custom-fabricated tail section. Extensive clay modelingâusing some 200 kilograms of clayâwas undertaken to refine the design, while structural rigidity was preserved through an integral rollover bar. Under the leadership of former Porsche designer Stephen Ferrarda and electrical engineer Stanley Daniels, the extraordinary conversion was completed in just three-and-a-half months.

Finished in period two-tone grey with bespoke spoilers, side skirts, graphics, and distinctive Centra alloy wheels, the prototype made its public debut at the 1982 British International Motor Show in Birmingham. Although limited-production plans were explored, the complexity of the roof mechanism ultimately prevented commercialization, leaving this example as the sole survivor of the project. Retaining its original drivetrain, the car combines unique coachbuilt design with the driving qualities of BMW's flagship grand tourer.

Following its press-tour duties, the car remained with creator Mike Gibbs until 1993, during which time the retractable roof was converted to its present fixed-glass configuration. Accompanied by an extensive history file, MOT records, and service documentation dating from 1989 to 2023, the BMW benefited from comprehensive restoration and refurbishment work in 2017 reportedly exceeding Â£26,000. Acquired by the present owner last year and showing just 19,315 miles at the time of cataloguing, this singular prototype represents a fascinating chapter in automotive innovation and a remarkably well-preserved precursor to the panoramic glass-roof concepts that would later become commonplace in modern grand touring automobiles.

THE ASTON MARTIN DB4

Classically proportioned and instantly recognizable from the moment of its introduction in 1958, the Touring-styled DB4 established a look that would survive, with only minor revisions, until 1970. A new design by Tadek Marek, the DB4's all-alloy, twin-overhead-camshaft six-cylinder engine featured 'square' bore and stroke dimensions of 92mm for a displacement of 3,670cc and developed its maximum output of 240bhp at 5,500rpm. The David Brown gearbox was a new four-speed all-synchromesh unit.

An immensely strong platform-type chassis replaced the DB2/4's multi-tubular spaceframe, the latter being considered incompatible with Touring's Superleggera body construction which employed its own lightweight tubular structure to support the aluminum-alloy body panels. The DB2/4's trailing-link ifs gave way to unequal-length wishbones while at the rear the DB4 sported a well-located live axle equipped with Watts linkage location instead of its predecessor's Panhard rod.

The DB4's peerless credentials as a Grand RoutiÃ©rÃ¨ were summed up thus by The Motor: 'Performance, controllability and comfort have been combined in the Aston Martin DB4 to make it a highly desirable car: one in which long journeys can be completed very quickly indeed with the minimum of risk or discomfort and the maximum of pleasure.'

Manufactured between October 1958 and June 1963, the DB4 developed through no fewer than five series. However, it should be made clear that the cars were not thus designated by the factory, this nomenclature having been suggested subsequently by the Aston Martin Owners Club to aid identification as the model evolved. The first series had already undergone a number of improvements, including the fitting of heavy-duty bumpers after the first 50 cars, before the second series arrived in January 1960. A front-hinged hood, bigger brake calipers and an enlarged sump were the major changes made on the Series II, while the third series featured separate rear lights, two hood stays, and a host of improvements to the interior fittings.

Its accompanying original RF.60 logbook shows that '619/R' was first registered (as 'EHS 66') to Messrs Sexton Son & Everard of Norwich on 1st May 1961. The second owner listed is Dawn Addams, believed to be the film and television actress of that name, who is perhaps best remembered for starring alongside Roger Moore in several episodes of the ITV series, 'The Saint', and appearing regularly in Thames Television's sitcom, 'Father, Dear Father'. 

Two further owners enjoyed the car before it came into the ownership of Michael Druce of Kintbury Garages Ltd who then sold the Aston to B.C. Fell in July 1969 (sales receipt on file). It should be noted that this logbook records a change of engine number from '673' to '637', though this may be merely the correction of a clerical error. 

 Bonhams sold the car the DB4 in May of 2019 to a subsequent UK owner who then imported it to the United States where it joined the present collection in 2021. Driven about 1,000 miles in the present ownership, it is reported that maintenance included oil changes and some new hoses have been done.

The car also comes with old/current V5/V5C documents, a quantity of expired tax discs and MoT certificates from 2002 to 2019, SORN paperwork, a quantity of photocopied literature, a workshop manual, and a parts book. Now titled in the US, it is the perfect machine for the next tour, rally, event, or local drive.

CORD E-300 EXPERIMENTAL PROTOTYPE

1929 was a record year for E.L. Cord with over 22,000 cars produced across his Auburn, Cord and Duesenberg marques. Wall Street's Black Tuesday Crash of October 29, 1929 came late in the year and had little effect on the full year results.

1930 on the other hand was brutal. Sales plummeted to under 14,000 cars. Profits evaporated. Auburn, Cord's moderately priced volume leader, retrenched, dropping all but its Lycoming straight eight powered 8-98. Cord's Front Drive (L-29) was introduced only two months before Black Tuesday and never sold more than a couple thousand cars a year. And the incomparable Duesenberg Model J sold in minute quantities to an exclusive market. 

1931, however, saw fortunes reverse, now under the umbrella of the Cord Corporation. Auburn sales of the 8-98 took off to over 34,000 units. Sales and profits hit records. E.L. Cord was hailed as a genius businessman. Cord and his managers shook off the malaise of the early 30's and looked for new opportunities.

One of those was a new, rationalized and less expensive Duesenberg that would take advantage of the Model J's exalted reputation while being accessible to a larger audience. It started life as experimental project E-277, later being reframed as project E-300 of which two prototypes (of five built) are known to survive. One of them is the car offered.

THE CAR OFFERED

Originally framed under project E-277 as a long wheelbase luxury car with power from a large displacement Lycoming BB L-head V-12, the E-277's mass made even more power necessary. The project added supercharging to deal with that and to make tangible the connection between it and supercharged Duesenberg racing car engines. Company engineering documents that survive support an estimate of 250 brake horsepower from 491 cubic inches.

Project E-277 was intended to be a major manifestation of Auburn Cord Duesenberg engineering, much more than badge engineering. Important features like four-wheel independent suspension were seriously considered, costed and engineered.

The company placed an order with coachbuilder LeBaron for five prototype bodies. Delivered in 1935, they were traditional coachwork constructed with hand-shaped panels over wood frames. By then, however, financial reality and the press to design, engineer, tool, and build the Cord 810 in a last-ditch attempt to salvage the company took priority. Project E-277 was shelved.

The hiatus lasted only a short time. When E.L. Cord during one of his increasingly infrequent visits to Auburn, Indiana spotted the five fully trimmed and painted prototype bodies from LeBaron he asked for them to be completed with at least one earmarked for his personal use. There was no time, or money, to complete the V-12 chassis but the engineers and designers in Auburn were creative, ingenious and skilled at adaptive reuse of components on hand.

It was likely at about this time that engineering project E-277 became E-300. It quickly took shape but instead of using the Lycoming V-12 the prototype chassis were shortened and a complete Cord 810 front subframe and drive train were welded on. The more compact and largely self-contained Cord 810 front wheel drive V-8 drivetrain resulted in a chassis wheelbase shortened by nearly a foot. 

Two known survivors and photographic evidence shows that chassis were completed with all five LeBaron prototype bodies: 7-passenger limousine, Berline sedan (E.L. Cord's choice), fastback sedan, phaeton sedan (convertible sedan) and cabriolet. Fenders and bodywork forward of the firewalls were designed and fabricated in Auburn using repurposed Cord 810 components with conventionally styled radiator grilles, 810 fenders with crank-operated retracting headlights. The rear fenders also were Cord 810-origin lengthened to complement the longer wheelbase design.

The design team in Auburn had some of the most gifted and visionary designers and stylists in the American automobile industry. Gordon Buehrig, Herb Newport, Phil Wright and LeBaron designer Ralph Roberts were prolific and forward-thinking visionaries who shaped many of the classic era's most innovative designs. Alex Tremulis, who arrived at Auburn in the early Thirties, learned his craft and refined his eye in the atelier of these visionaries. They led, collaborated, sketched and laid out the E-300 project's coachwork even though they were limited by resources and finances to using available components.

Tremulis contributed the grille, suggested by some as being a representation of the grilles used by the racing cars of Fred and Augie Duesenberg. While fenders came directly from Cord 810 parts supply the designers added running boards that tapered into the front fenders and related visually to the familiar classic coachwork of the Duesenberg Model J. Chrome-trimmed longitudinal hood side vents resolved engine compartment cooling with a hint of Buehrig's Cord 810 hood. A particularly effective detail is the vestigial spline down the body's rear deck cover. A clever feature is the integrated folding top and rear deck top boot cover, an ingenious mechanism probably initiated by LeBaron that foretold "revolutionary" folding top systems of the 1980's and 90's.

Both surviving Experimental E-300 Cord Prototypes used FC-series centrifugally supercharged 289 cubic inch engines that made 170hp in Cord 812s. Both use standard Cord 810/812 pre-selector 4-speed manual transmissions. The Harrah Collection documented the history of its Cord Experimental Berline in its usual thorough and transparent way including interviews with E.L. Cord and his son, Charlie and E.L. Cord stated two of the experimental cars were crashed and destroyed. The fate of the last of the five is unknown.

After Cord Corporation's 1937 receivership this LeBaron cabriolet became the property of company president Lucius B. Manning. Manning, who one prior owner of this delectable cabriolet noted, "was known to be more fond of a sharp pencil than leather and steel" became president of America Airlines, bringing the E-300 Cabriolet with him to Chicago. Later owners include an unnamed woman in Florida, Arthur Medlor in Pawtucket, Rhode Island, Wilbur Sanders in Michigan, Thel Horn also in Michigan and then John Baeke's father from whom it passed to Baeke. The present owner acquired it in 2013.

Contemporary photos in the 1950s show it to have been in badly deteriorated and neglected condition but largely complete and a succession of owners through the middle of the last century while not knowing its history appreciated its style, design and uniqueness, a car they appreciated as special without knowing why.

The present owners began restoration, taking extreme efforts to document and reproduce the original paint colors from under brackets, the body tag and bolted joints. Similar efforts went into reproducing the original upholstery, carpet and top materials and colors. These efforts are documented in an extensive library of restoration photographs. In addition, a voluminous file of original document copies from the period and engineering analysis of materials, costs, component availability and accounting of obsolete inventory compiled by former owner Dr. John Baeke is an insightful recounting of the engineering and financial efforts of a company in extremis and responsibly trying to prolong its viability.

Resplendent in a distinctive red livery with hints of orange tint, the interior is beige leather matching the top cloth color. The engine, chassis, frame, and undercarriage are restored to concours condition. The instrument panel, with its engine-turned finish, is populated by an array of clear, crisp gauges. Elaborately grained wood embellishes the dashboard and door cappings, a flourish that highlights LeBaron's craftsmanship.

The restoration was completed in 2021 and has never been shown, displayed, or exhibited, giving the next owner the opportunity to expand upon its unique history, design, style and performance. It is a magnificent, beautiful, singular automobile derived from some of the most creative, innovative, ingenious minds of the classic era: E.L. Cord, Gordon Buehrig, Herb Newport, Alex Tremulis, Phil Wright and Ralph Roberts of LeBaron, Harold Ames of Duesenberg.

It is, in the true meaning of the word, unique.

THE PACKARD 11TH SERIES TWELVE

The Packard Eleventh Series V12 is a quintessential American classic of the early 1930s. Making its debut in late 1933 for the 1934 model year (following Packard's typical off-sequence model schedule), it was essentially an evolution of the outgoing 10th Series. The 11th Series featured new fenders and other stylistic refinements giving a fuller appearance, enhancing the already elegant form of the 10th Series, and resulting in what many consider the quintessential Classic Era design. On the one hand, the leading manufacturers of the day competed to see which could be declared "King of the Hill" when it came to the multi-cylinder luxury car market. Cadillac, Auburn, Franklin, Lincoln and Pierce-Arrow all brought out 12-cylinder models in the early to mid-1930s, just as the Depression took a stranglehold on the world's economy. As Packard was generally acknowledged to have marketed the world's first production V12 with the 1916 "Twin Six", when their later twelve was introduced in 1932, it quickly became a standard by which others were measured. Its 67Â° V-block gave it the kind of smooth balance expected of a Packard and indeed when standing by one at idle, it may be difficult to discern if it is running or not, such is its level of refinement.

On the other hand, Packard styling for 1934 was a fleeting moment of perfection as industry priorities were changing rapidly. The market was demanding quieter smoother riding cars and drivers were expecting cars with lighter steering and better brakes. Wheels began to shrink â the stately 20" quickly gave way to 17" wheels and fenders gained skirting to hide the empty space as wheels shrunk. Up to 1934, the bodies were basically designed for the earlier 1930-32 era cars and the fenders and noses were changed to blend the two, somehow managing to retain the early 1930s elegance.

THE CAR OFFERED

This 1934 Packard 1108 is a gorgeous example of the rarely seen Style No. 4070 Convertible Sedan. It is one of just 960 11th Series Twelves built, and the gorgeous Convertible Sedan coachwork is highly desirable and rarely seen with only about a dozen examples surviving. 

This example was in the collection of Packard enthusiast John Own Bohmer for some six decades. As documented in Bohmer's book A Man and his Cars, this rare Packard was in Minneapolis in the post-WWII era, owned by an Alaskan dentist who no doubt enjoyed it sparingly given the limited driving season up there. The car was eventually sold on to a friend of Bohmer's who drove the unrestored open Packard as daily driver. An enthusiastic motorist, he was also apparently an equally enthusiastic drinker and one night combined his two loves. Driving his rare Convertible Sedan late one night, he crashed the car at high speedâbut managed to survive. It was at this point the Bohmer was finally able to acquire the Packard he had been chasing...albeit at a discount but in need of restoration. Purchasing the car for "a grand", the Packard was loaded up and brought home.

Sitting as a soon-to-be-started project from a decade, the restoration was started in earnest in 1977. Photos of the car prior to restoration are on file. Initially working to restore the car himselfâand buying a disassembled '34 Twelve Touring Sedan as a part carâBohmer set out working to bring the old girl back to her former glory. It was soon discovered that the 'custom' in 'Custom Dietrich' meant the parts car was not a final solution and set out to have full restoration completed by marque experts. The professional restoration took three years to complete and is documented in receipts and records. Once completed in 1982, the restored Custom Convertible Sedan was shown at the Packard meet in Warren, Ohio where it promptly won first place. 

Maintained as part of Bohmer's expansive Classic Era collection until he passed away in 2022, the current owner acquired the car the next year.

The hallmark of a good restoration is not how it looks when finished but decades later, and this example demonstrates how a quality restoration can ripen with time. This Packard remains a worthy centerpiece to virtually any collection, with style and substance in abundance, equally capable of further concours accolades or returning many miles of sublime touring pleasure.

THE RAUCH & LANG

Among America's most respected carriage builders, Rauch & Lang successfully bridged the transition from horse-drawn transport to the emerging motor age. Established in Cleveland, Ohio, in 1884 by Jacob Rauch and Charles Lang, the firm earned an enviable reputation for producing finely crafted, luxurious carriages for an affluent clientele. Recognizing the potential of electric propulsion, the company entered the automobile market in 1903 as a Buffalo Electric agent before introducing its own Rauch & Lang-branded electric cars in 1905. By acquiring the Hertner Electric Company in 1907, Rauch & Lang gained control over the manufacture of its motors and controllers, allowing nearly every major component to be produced in-house and cementing its reputation as one of America's premier electric automobile manufacturers.

By 1916, Rauch & Lang offered an extensive range of sophisticated electric cars in multiple wheelbases and body styles, catering to discerning urban motorists who valued refinement, reliability, and ease of operation. With prices ranging from $2,600 to $4,500âat a time when Ford's Model T sold for less than $400âthese elegant electrics occupied the very top tier of the American automobile market. Their silent operation, absence of smoke or vibration, and uncomplicated controls made them especially popular among wealthy city residents. Following its merger with the Baker Motor Vehicle Company, Rauch & Lang continued production into the early 1920s before the widespread adoption of self-starting gasoline automobiles ultimately brought the era of luxury electric cars to a close.

THE CAR OFFERED

Offered here is a beautifully well-preserved 1916 Rauch & Lang Model BX6 Brougham, believed to be one of fewer than 1,000 examples produced during the company's later years. Riding on the 92-inch wheelbase and fitted with handsome fully enclosed Brougham coachwork, this example originally carried a list price of $2,800âmore than eight times the cost of a contemporary Model T Runabout.

The car boasts extraordinary provenance, having been acquired in the late 1940s by noted collector Paul Kelsey for what would become the Kelsey Antique Auto Collection. Opened in 1954 in the Missouri Ozarks, the museum became a well-known roadside attraction, and this Rauch & Lang remained a prominent exhibit throughout its history. Following the museum's closure in the 1990s, the car remained in the Kelsey family, resulting in over 75 years of continuous family ownership before entering its current collection.

Remarkably, the BX6 has never been restored and is believed to retain its original paint and finishes, making it an exceptionally rare preservation example. The blue broadcloth interior remains beautifully intact and is complemented by a set of period custom-fitted cloth slipcovers, made decades ago to protect the upholstery and still accompanying the car today. Their continued presence contributes to the authentic character developed over generations of careful stewardship.

The thoughtfully designed interior exemplifies the ingenuity of early electric automobiles. Without the intrusion of a conventional engine compartment, the cabin offers distinctive parlor-style seating for four. The driver occupies the rear bench and controls the car with a folding tiller, facing two rear-facing passenger seatsâone swiveling and one fixed. The controls for speed, braking, and reverse are conveniently positioned, while the dashboard is fitted with a charming array of Rauch & Lang-branded Warner instruments monitoring speed, mileage, voltage, amperage, and battery consumption. A Waltham clock remains fitted, while delightful period details include a full-width interior rearview mirror above the windshield and even a handheld vanity mirror housed in a dedicated pocket beside the driver's position.

Since leaving the Kelsey family, the car's remarkable originality has been carefully maintained rather than restored. It has been fitted with six modern 12-volt deep-cycle batteries and new tires to facilitate operation, while the original battery boxes remain intactâan exceptionally uncommon survival. The car is reported to be running and driving, although, following its long-term museum preservation, some routine recommissioning should be anticipated before regular use.

Highly original early electric automobiles are seldom encountered, particularly those retaining such an extraordinary degree of authenticity and documented long-term ownership. Equally suited to preservation-class concours competition, museum exhibition, or events celebrating the history of alternative propulsion, this remarkably intact Rauch & Lang stands as an evocative reminder that the electric automobile's history extends back well over a century, representing one of the finest surviving examples of America's pioneering luxury electric motorcars.

THOMAS MODEL 18

In common with many of his contemporary automobile manufacturers, Erwin R. Thomas began by building bicycles, first as an employee of Lozier building the Cleveland bicycle and later on his own in Buffalo, New York. His first products were kits to motorize bicycles and at one point Thomas was the largest maker of single-cylinder air-cooled engines in the country. The Thomas Auto Bi motorized bicycle set a record across the U.S. in 1905. It took 48 days.

Automobile manufacturing began in 1902 with the Model 17 with a 2-speed planetary gearbox. Although powered by a single-cylinder engine, it was a full-size automobile available either as a runabout or a rear entrance tonneau. It was succeeded in 1903 by the Model 18, also a single but now with a 3-speed sliding gear transmission.

The Model 18 was a large, comfortable automobile with a full-size body in what Thomas literature described as the King of Belgium style indicative of the curved style bodies that Thomas would go on to be famous for. Its single cylinder engine displaced a prodigious 106 cubic inches. Its 3-speed transmission was an important step forward with Thomas literature citing "the foreign system of speed change shifting gear.... The intermediate speed, equivalent to largely increased power, is a real necessity for touring, bad roads and long hills". Highly developed, beautifully finished and thoughtfully designed, the Thomas Model 18 is the pinnacle of single cylinder automobiles.

In the 1960s, the fiberglass kit-car craze was taking hold in America. Versatile and inexpensive, fiberglass was easy for the average enthusiast to use, and custom car builders, racers, and hot-rodders turned to it as a viable alternative to sheet metal to turn their dreams into reality. Able to be molded into any shape imaginable, fiberglass build-your-own car kits sprang up to suit an endless variety of donor cars.

The most distinctive car of the genre emerged from the California workshops of Bruce F. Meyers. Mr. Meyers was an engineer, boat builder, artist, tinkerer, surfer, and amateur desert racer who sparked the kit-car craze of the 60s. Eschewing the typical sports car and "Kustom" styles favored by other kit manufacturers, Meyers designed and built a VW Beetle-based machine that was equally at home on the beach, the street, or racing through the desert â the original Dune Buggy. Drawing from his boat building experience, Meyers created the first dune buggy using a shortened VW drivetrain fitted to fiberglass monocoque body with a mix of VW and Chevy truck suspension parts. He named it the "Manx" after the stubby, short-tailed Manx cat.

Donor Beetles were cheap, plentiful, and readily tunable which gave the light and nimble Manx astonishing performance both on and off-road. Bruce Meyers' little buggy first made headlines in 1967 when it set the four-wheel Baja Peninsula speed record, and then again when it won the 1967 Mexican 1000 desert race (the predecessor to the Baja 1000), proving its mettle as a serious competition car. Sales exploded and soon scores of copies began flooding the market as the dune buggy craze took off. However, the copycats never captured the magic of the original Meyers Manx, which remained in production for years, and is now a bona fide cult-classic, and authentic Meyers originals continue to be prized by enthusiasts worldwide. In 2019, Bruce Meyers Meyers, who passed his legendary brand on to the current caretakers in 2019, launching a new Meyers Manx to carry on his legacy. 

Even after 60 years, the Meyers Manx remains a one-of-a-kind American icon. The company has been recently reborn, now delivering turn-key, Remastered Manxes with new components and a refined version of Bruce's original body design. The full range includes a four-seat Resorter model as well as a Manx with an aircraft-inspired radial engine. This example was acquired by the Meyers Manx Heritage Collection has been cared for and updated by their team. Powered by a punched-out 1,776cc VW flat four, it has been stanced and lowered with an eye toward blasting across the sand dunes and beaches. Fitted with knobby Baja Pro tires, it is stunningly finished in Green Metalflake Gelcoat over low-back white vinyl bucked seats. The teak deck behind the seats has been freshly redone and a new set of Coco mats adorn the footwells. While the collection is retaining a handful of other special buggies, it is time for "Lowrider" to go to new caretakers where it can continue to deliver more smiles per mile.

THE JAGUAR XJ220

The words "supercar" and "sensational" are often found in combination and are never more justifiably so than in the case of Jaguar's fabulous XJ220. Worthy successor to the multiple Le Mans-winning C-Type and D-Type Jaguars of the 1950s, the XJ220 commanded headlines just as its illustrious forebears had done in previous decades when it burst upon an astonished world in October 1991.

Planning for Jaguar's proposed 200mph supercar had begun in the mid-1980s â design work proceeding largely in the project team's spare time â and finally bore fruit when the prototype was exhibited at the British International Motor Show in Birmingham in October 1988, only four months after Jaguar's sixth outright victory at the Le Mans 24 Hours. Clothed in aluminum bodywork styled by Keith Helfet, the XJ220 concept featured an upswept tail, deeply scalloped side air intakes, and flush headlight covers that dropped into the nose to reveal fixed lenses beneath.

The reception was overwhelming: showgoers reportedly offered blank cheques on the spot, though none were accepted by Jaguar at that stage. On the strength of this response, Jaguar committed to a limited production run, initially reported at between 220 and 350 cars, and turned to its long-standing endurance-racing partner, Tom Walkinshaw Racing (TWR), to develop and construct the car â Jaguar itself lacking the capacity to build it in-house.

The formal order book opened in late 1989, at which point Jaguar began taking firm reservations against a deposit of Â£50,000; some 1,500 deposits are reported to have been received. By the time these contracts were signed, the revised production specification â including the replacement of the concept's 6.2-liter V12 and four-wheel-drive system â had already been disclosed, meaning buyers committed their deposits with knowledge of the car's definitive rear-wheel-drive, twin-turbocharged V6 configuration.

The XJ220 survived Jaguar's acquisition by Ford in 1989, but by the time it entered production in 1992 it differed substantially from the original show car. In place of the prototype's V12, production cars used a more powerful Cosworth-designed 3.5-liter twin-turbo V6, derived from the unit fitted to the XJR-11 sports-racer, producing 542bhp; the prototype's four-wheel drive and adaptive suspension were likewise dropped in the interest of production feasibility. An eventual VAT-inclusive price of nearly Â£403,000 only reinforced the model's exclusivity.

With the rev limiter raised and catalytic converters removed, the XJ220 held the record for the world's fastest production car between 1992 and 1998, achieving 217.1mph at the NardÃ² Ring in Italy; with emissions equipment fitted, Formula One driver Martin Brundle recorded 212mph in period testing. The 0â100mph sprint was accomplished in a reported 7.9 seconds.

Production of the Jaguar XJ220 concluded in 1994 after approximately 297 chassis had been completed, of which 281 were ultimately assembled into complete vehicles. Of these, 268 were standard road cars, while Tom Walkinshaw Racing converted a select number into specialized derivatives, including six XJ220 S road carsâone built as a unique commission for a private clientâfour XJ220 C competition cars, and three XJ220-N Group N examples. 

The remaining 16 chassis were retained as spares. As with many limited-production supercars of the era, published production figures vary slightly depending on whether prototypes, incomplete chassis, and competition variants are included in the total.

THE CAR OFFERED

Chassis no. 003 (VIN. SAJJEAEX8AX220769) began life as a standard XJ220 road car, finished in Spa Silver over grey leather, before being sent to TWR for preparation to Group N specification â a category intended to remain as close to the road-going car as possible, retaining its power windows, air conditioning & heat, headlights, turn signals, and windscreen wipers. It was the third and final of the three Group N cars built by Tom Walkinshaw Racing, commissioned, together with its two sister cars, by the Italian Top Run race team at the instigation of the Benetton family for the 1993 Campionato Italiano Supercar GT season. 

Chassis no. 001 and 002 were finished in the team's white livery with light and dark blue side stripes and assigned race numbers 11 and 12 respectively; car #11 was subsequently repainted in Martini livery. Chassis no. 003, by contrast, was retained as the team's backup car and never raced, and it remains finished in its original Spa Silver to this day. Unlike its two campaigned sister cars, it is understood to have never turned a wheel in competition, remaining a team spare before passing to a new owner in 1994.

The car retains its factory-correct mechanical specification, including the larger turbocharger housings unique to the N-variant cars, a five-speed manual transaxle with limited-slip differential, and a full competition interior comprising OMP seats, Schroth six-point harnesses, an integrated roll cage, a three-spoke Personal steering wheel, and an AiM digital dash. A TWR identification tag in the driver's door jamb confirms the car as chassis 003 with a build date of September 1993; the factory VIN is stamped in the engine bay. The odometer is non-functional, and total mileage is not recorded.

Despite its purpose-built competition specification, chassis no. 003 retains a number of road-derived styling and aerodynamic elements carried over from the standard production car, including a front air dam, trunk-mounted rear spoiler, and retractable headlight covers â details that lend the Group N cars a distinctly production-based silhouette despite their racing purpose. The car rides on multi-piece BBS wheels shod in Hoosier competition tires, with stopping power provided by a Brembo disc brake system featuring slotted, ventilated rotors.

Its original Spa Silver paint survives beneath a vinyl livery applied in 2024 for display at the New York International Auto Show â a reinterpretation of the works team's white-and-blue scheme, carrying period sponsor graphics and race number 13, and fully removable to reveal the car's original factory finish. Despite its track-honed specification, chassis 003 retains its road-going equipment, underscoring its usability on the street as much as on circuit. 

As one of only three Group N cars built, and the sole example reportedly to never campaigned in period, chassis no. 003 represents a rare opportunity to acquire a genuine piece of Jaguar XJ220 history.

Please note that the vehicle is being offered on a bill of sale. The odometer is inoperative, and the engine exhibits a rough idle. According to the marque specialist who most recently serviced the car, the rough idle is attributed to the need for a MoTeC engine management system.

THE PICCHIO

Picchio is a small but highly respected Italian constructor specializing in sports-racing prototypes. Based in Ancarano, Italy, the company was founded in 1989 with the involvement of legendary engineer Giotto Bizzarrini, the man famous for helping create icons such as the Ferrari 250 GTO and Bizzarrini sports cars. The company was established to design and build lightweight racing prototypes, and its first major success came with the Picchio SR2, a carbon-fiber sports racer powered by BMW inline-six engines. These cars competed successfully in European prototype racing before Picchio expanded into North America. For American enthusiasts, Picchio is best known for the D-USA/SRP II program. In 2002, working with North American distributor Armando Trentini and G&W Motorsports, Picchio developed the D-USA prototype for Grand-Am's SRP II category. The BMW-powered cars earned victories and championship success, with drivers including Darren Law and Andy Lally.

What makes Picchio notable is that it belongs to the tradition of specialist Italian racing constructors such as Dallara, Lola Cars, and Osellaâsmall engineering-focused firms that build purpose-designed competition machines rather than production road cars. Despite its modest size, Picchio developed carbon-fiber prototypes, Daytona Prototypes, hill-climb specials, and experimental road-car projects over more than three decades.

THE CAR OFFERED

The Picchio D-USA represents one of the more remarkable entries in American sports car racing history â an Italian-built, BMW-powered prototype introduced into the Rolex Grand Am Sports Car Series by a small, determined team, which proceeded to challenge the class establishment with a consistency and pace few anticipated. Chassis 1-02 D USA is the original car of that program, the first Picchio built specifically to Grand-Am SRP II regulations and homologated for the United States market.
In 2002, Bizzarrini and Picchio gave Armando Trentini exclusivity to introduce the D-USA variant â a closed-cockpit configuration designed around Grand-Am's SRP II category â and entrusted its campaign to G&W Motorsports, managed by 1990 Le Mans winner Price Cobb.

The car was powered by a race-prepared BMW inline-six of 3.0 liters, mated to a Hewland sequential gearbox. The chassis, as with all Picchio prototypes of the era, was a reinforced steel tube frame clad in fiberglass and kevlar bodywork, with pushrod suspension at both ends and AP Racing braking. At roughly 750 kilograms in race trim, it was a genuinely formidable SRP II weapon â light, responsive, and purpose-built for the circuits of the American championship calendar.

The driving program assembled by G&W for 2002 was of serious caliber. Darren Law, already a proven Rolex Series competitor and recent GT class champion, led the effort alongside Andy Lally â one of American sports car racing's most naturally gifted and versatile pilots. Together, Law and Lally extracted the maximum from the D-USA across the full season, recording multiple podium finishes including second-place results at Miami Homestead, California Speedway at Fontana, and Phoenix International Raceway. The car also ran in the Rolex 24 at Daytona, finishing sixth in class. At season's end, Law stood second in the SRP II driver's championship â the highest result any Picchio chassis had achieved in North America to that point. In addition to Darren Law's overall 2nd place season result the car also placed second in the SRP II class.

Armando Trentini also shared the car on selected rounds, and the trio combined for an outright class victory at the Six Hours of Circuit Mont-Tremblant, the first international race win for the D-USA program. 

The 2002 season established Picchio's credibility in American prototype racing and laid the foundation for the DP2, which followed in 2003 and made Picchio the first foreign manufacturer approved by Grand-Am to construct a Daytona Prototype. Chassis 1-02 D USA is therefore not merely a successful race car â it is the proof-of-concept from which that entire chapter was built.

G&W Motorsports dominated the 2003 Grand-Am Rolex Sports Car Series in the Sports Racing Prototype II (SRP II) class. Steve Marshall won the SRP II Drivers' Championship. The car was a frequent front-runner, racking up class wins and podiums across the 12-race season finishing first in the SRP II Class. 
Restored in 2013 by Shawn Bayliff's race shop and presented in a striking yellow and blue livery, Chassis 1-02 D USA has received over $30,000 in updates and service under current ownership to ensure it remains in great running order and eligible for a growing calendar of prestigious historic events in both North America and Europe â among them the Classic 24 Hours at Daytona and the Velocity Invitational. As one of only a handful of D-USA examples ever produced, and the original chassis of the program, it holds a singular and distinguished place in the history of Picchio in America.

THE NISSAN SKYLINE

To an entire generation of car enthusiasts, the Nissan Skyline legend starts with the high-tech R32 GT-R of the 1990s, but the iconic Skyline name stretches clear back to 1957, under the Prince Motor Company banner. The later S50 generation began the Skyline's competition success story in 1964, further elevating the model's lore. Through multiple developments of the Skyline, the GT, 2000GT, GT-B, GT-X, RS, and GT-R monikers graced the bootlids of these desirable high-performance machines.

The definitive model of the Skyline's 7th generation is the GTS-R (HR31). While quite rare, its significance in Skyline history should not be overlooked, as it marked the debut of the now-legendary RB20DET-R engine. Displacing just over 2 liters, the compact inline-six features twin overhead cams, electronic fuel injection, and an intercooled turbocharger. In road trim, the engine was modestly rated at 207bhp, with at least twice that available in Group A racing trim, and even more in the hands of tuners. Complementing that superb engine was a tuned chassis to handle the additional power, and a crisp, understated 2-door coupe body with just the right touch of aggression. To qualify for Group A rules, Nissan produced 823 examples of the GTS-R, which served an important development role for the all-conquering R32 that followed. The HR31 proved itself in the heat of battle by taking the Japanese Touring Car Championship in 1989, while Jimmy Richards steered his HR31 to the hotly contested Australian Touring Car title in 1990.

THE CAR OFFERED

NISMO (Nissan Motorsports) began using the HR31 in 1987, and the car had a steady presence at the sharp end of the field in Group A racing for several years. Our featured car, chassis HR31-128388, was prepared to Group A specs by Kazuyushi Hoshino's Impul/Nismo team and is notable for being the very first Skyline touring car to wear the now famous blue and white Calsonic livery â made so by the R32 Skyline GT-R "Godzilla" Group A car. In 1988, this car achieved a pair of top 5 finishes (driven by touring car specialists Moto Kitano and Takao Wada), along with three DNFs. The following season, with Kitano joined by Hoshino, the car started on the front row in 5 of 6 races (with 4 poles) taking one win at Nishi-Sendai Hi-Land Raceway, and a spectacular fight through the field from 36th on the grid to 6th overall at Suzuka.

For the past 30 years, the famous Calsonic HR31 has lived a quiet life as part of the consignor's private collection. It is the subject of a thorough refurbishment, completed in July 2024. Details of the project include restoring the bodyshell in that glorious bright blue and recreating the original Calsonic livery and markings. The RB20DET-R engine was reportedly rebuilt by a NISMO engineer in 2023, which included repairs to the special magnesium intake manifold, freshened radiator and intercooler, and more. Additionally, the gearbox was inspected, the clutch and brake hydraulics freshened, new brake discs fitted, air jacks checked, and many other details tended to return the car to running condition. As with any racing machine, a full technical inspection is recommended prior to embarking on any on-track activities.

In a special event held at Fuji Speedway in July 2024, the restored Calsonic NISMO HR31 was reunited with Kazuyoshi Hoshino, where he conducted some interviews beside his old racecar. The car was taken out for some demonstration laps by its demo driver, further sorting the car for circuit use. Soggy conditions prevented him from fully uncorking the Skyline, but video was taken of the demo driver and Wada, on board his restored H30, swapping places for the cameras and savoring a chance to be back behind the wheel of a legendary racing car.

Wonderfully restored to its as-raced specification, this incredibly special Skyline GTS-R Gr.A represents a significant milestone in Nissan's illustrious motorsport history, presenting an exceptionally rare opportunity to acquire the very first Skyline to wear the now iconic Calsonic blue livery.

THE DIABLO GT

The culmination of a decade of Diablo development, the Lamborghini Diablo GT stands as one of the most uncompromising road cars ever to emerge from Sant'Agata Bolognese. Unveiled at the Geneva Auto Show in March 1999 as a homologation-inspired, track-focused evolution of the legendary Diablo, it was produced in a strictly limited run of just 80 examples â though 83 were ultimately delivered before the entire production run sold out in January 2000. It remains among the rarest and most coveted Lamborghinis of the modern era.

At its heart lies a 6.0-liter naturally aspirated V12 producing 575 horsepower, driving the rear wheels exclusively through a five-speed manual gearbox. In a deliberate departure from the all-wheel-drive Diablo VT, Lamborghini stripped the GT to its essence â extensive carbon fiber construction, dramatically widened bodywork, a functional roof-mounted ram-air intake, and a purposefully spartan cockpit all in pursuit of one goal: maximum performance with minimum compromise. An Individual Intake System with a dedicated throttle body per cylinder, paired with Lamborghini's Exhaust Noise Control System, ensured the engine breathed â and sounded â unlike any other Diablo. The result was a 0â100 km/h time of 3.5 seconds and a top speed of 338 km/h, making it the most formidable road-going Diablo ever produced.

Visually, the GT is impossible to mistake. Flared fenders, unique OZ Racing wheels, NACA ducts, a prominent rear diffuser, and a high-gloss carbon fiber rear wing transformed the already dramatic Diablo into something altogether more extreme. The GT's development directly informed both the subsequent Diablo VT 6.0 and the track-only GTR, cementing its place as the technical apex of the entire Diablo lineage.

Launched at approximately $300,000, the GT was immediately recognized as a future collector's piece â and time has validated that judgment entirely. For the serious collector, it stands not only as the purest expression of Lamborghini's pre-MurciÃ©lago era, but as one of the defining performance cars of the late 1990s and a true landmark in the marque's storied history.

THE CAR OFFERED

VIN. ZA9DE21A0YLA12561, the 74th of just 80 Diablo GTs produced, represents one of the rarest and most significant road cars ever to emerge from Lamborghini's Sant'Agata factory. Originally delivered in rare and striking Black Rage-over-Nero leather bucket seats with carbon fiber trim, this exceptional example embodies the uncompromising philosophy that established the GT as the ultimate expression of the legendary Diablo lineage.

Occupying a singular position in Lamborghini history, the Diablo GT stands as the final and most focused evolution of the original Diablo platform. Developed before the arrival of the Audi-era VT 6.0, it serves as both the culmination of Lamborghini's raw, analog supercar tradition and a bridge to the marque's modern era. With its naturally aspirated 6.0-liter V12, gated five-speed manual gearbox, rear-wheel-drive configuration, and absence of modern electronic intervention, the GT delivers an increasingly rare level of driver engagement that few contemporary performance cars can replicate.

Showing just 14,208 kilometers at the time of cataloging, chassis 12561 has remained under the stewardship of its current owner for the past 19 years and is offered with a U.S. title. Professionally maintained by master Lamborghini mechanic Steve Gleanor at Driven Exotics, the clutch was replaced at 12,225 kms.

Accompanying the vehicle are its rare factory leather briefcase, owner's manual, service records, one key with remote, a set of installed racing harnesses, optional back up camera and complete factory OEM tool kit in leather bag.

More than a quarter century after its introduction, the Diablo GT is widely regarded as one of the defining supercars of its era and among the most collectible Lamborghinis ever built. Combining extraordinary rarity, exhilarating performance, and unmistakable visual presence, chassis 12561 presents a compelling opportunity to acquire one of the finest expressions of Lamborghini's V12 heritage landmark model that remains every bit as captivating, visceral, and uncompromising today as when it first left Sant'Agata Bolognese.

SCUDERIA TORO ROSSO

Today's Formula 1 Racing Bulls team was known from 2006-2019 as Scuderia Toro Rosso - and it grew from the takeover by Red Bull energy drinks co-owner Dietrich Mateschitz of the former Minardi team, of Faenza, Italy. Minardi had competed at this top level of motor sport from 1985 to 2005. It had been a team which enjoyed little success, while counting future World Champion Driver Fernando Alonso amongst its alumni, together with such subsequent Grand Prix race winners as Giancarlo Fisichella, Alessandro Nannini, Jaarno Trulli and Mark Weber.

The Toro Rosso team's 2019 STR14 car was designed around the proven rear end configuration of the previous year's Red Bull-Honda. Its new team technical director Jody Eggington oversaw the design's completion and race development through the 2019 season, which saw it score two podium finishes which were the first achieved by the team since Sebastian Vettel had won the 2008 Italian Grand Prix in one of its earlier cars.

The Red Bull rear end comprised suspension and gearbox - the transmission assembly having been designed around the preceding Renault power unit instead of the Honda V6 which had a split turbocharger system. This meant that the gearbox was unnecessarily long, making the Toro Rosso the third-longest Formula 1 car in the entire 2019 field. At the front end the inboard suspension components were used from the preceding Red Bull car system.

Technical Director Eggington said that "It all worked quite well" - including the front end aerodynamic treatment which was quite different from Red Bull practice. Built for essential simplicity and practicality, the STR14 's competitiveness tended to diminish through the second half of the season, despite which it had a far better development rate than its predecessors. Over the season the STR14's average qualifying pace was assessed to be 1.6sec adrift of the dominant Mercedes. 

These overall traits were well demonstrated by the broad range of circuits at which the car performed well. Such venues as Baku, Monaco, Silverstone and Monza each made very different demands upon competing chassis.

THE CAR OFFERED

This startlingly beautiful modern-era Formula 1 car is offered here is not only a much-raced team car from the lengthy 2019 Formula 1 World Championship season, but also a podium place-winning car, having been driven by the French star Pierre Gasly to finish second in that year's Brazilian Grand Prix at Interlagos, Sao Paulo.

This particular chassis was driven in the opening nine rounds of that 2019 Formula 1 World Championship seasons Grands Prix races by rapidly improving British Thai hopeful Alex Albon. In it he scored World Championship points in the year's Monaco (8th) and German (6th) GPs. When he was promoted into the 'parent' Red Bull team, French newcomer Pierre Gasly took over for the final min rounds of the Championship - scoring points in the Belgian (9th), Singapore (8th), Japanese (7th) and Mexican (9th) GPs before his singular second place overall to join winner Max Verstappen of Red Bull and third placement Carlos Sainz of McLaren upon the podium.

The type's other podium finishes achieved in the rain at Hockenheim, Germany, where Danil Kvyat had finished third. In Germany, Kvyat's contemporary Toro Rosso team-mate Alex Albon had seemed set for a podium finish after a great wet-weather drive. And overall these Toro Rosso STR14s were regular lower order points scorers.

The car's original power unit was a Honda RA619H 90-degree V6-cylinder engine, driving through an 8-speed gearbox with carbon-composite main case, longitudinally-mounted, with a hydraulic power shift. The monocoque chassis itself is another sophisticated carbon-composite molding. Front suspension is by composite wishbones with push-rod activated inboard torsion bar springs and dampers. At the rear further carbon-composite wishbones located the road wheels while inboard suspension was actuated by a pull-rod system, with torsion bars and dampers. The braking system featured 6-pot Toro Rosso/Red Bull Technology calibers, clasping advanced and ventilated carbon discs. 

While this handsome display car lacks an engineâHonda Motorsports retains them, its rear-end integrity is maintained by a fabricated steel frame which is attached to the forward monocoque fuselage tub and the rear gearbox casing via billet machined components. The pedal box and associated hydraulic components including the brake master cylinders, hydraulic reservoirs and steering rack are all included, and the composite steering column remains in place.

Notably, we understand that this most attractive show car is accompanied by two steering wheels - one race-spec and the other for transport duties - a Toro Rosso protective cover, spare front wing, and two additional sets of wheel rims and tires, plus sockets. As a largely complete machine, one could enjoy it as a hallmark display piece within their collector or endeavor to install a suitable power unit and fulfill one's Formula 1 driver dreams. Amongst such display pieces, those with genuine points-scoring race history are quite rare. Those which carried their drivers to podium-place finishes (first three) are very rare. When rarity dictates desirability, it is evident that this is indeed a most mouth-watering modern-era collector's item.

THE JETCAR OFFERED

As recounted in an October 1960 Hot Rod Magazine article by Ray Brock, Dr. Ostich gathered a group of friends for a free steak dinner in 1957 and put to them and their hot-rodding skills the idea of building a jet-powered car capable of pushing the Land Speed Record over 500mph. The idea was debated. Resources were assessed and one element appeared as critical: tires.

A 20" outside diameter tire at 500mph rotates at 8,400rpm, a speed that would subject the tire to a centripetal acceleration of about 20,000 Gs. In other words, the tire would be torn asunder. Dr. Ostich needed a solution and approached Firestone which agreed to see if they could come up with a wheel and tire combination that would sustain a linear speed of 500mph without coming apart.

On the assumption that was possible, Dr. Ostich put up the money, gathered his team of part time LSR rodders and set them to work.

Over the next two years with a target of being on The Salt at Bonneville in 1960 they set to work. A General Electric J47-19 turbojet, designed for a set of four on a Convair B-36D strategic bomber that also used six Pratt & Whitney R-4360-53 Wasp Major radial piston engine in pusher configuration was selected. The J47-19 turbojet generated 5,200 pounds force thrust at 7,950rpm. A community of volunteers joined together under Dr. Ostich's leadership and encouragement and the "Flying Caduceus" began to take shape.

Its 4-foot diameter cylindrical structure was built from steel tubing. It was covered in an aluminum skin. The cockpit sat forward and low behind an aluminum nose, a beak might be a better description, flanked by two air intake ducts. The four-wheel independent suspension was made from '60 Chevrolet front suspension components.

Even on the vast, flat, surface of the Bonneville salt flats braking was needed and the Flying Caduceus got four 14" diameter discs brakes with Halibrand calipers. An 8-foot diameter ribbon parachute provided high speed braking but wasn't needed until air resistance quickly retarded the Flying Caduceus from its projected top speed. In the initial configuration there was no crosswind stabilizing fin something added in later attempts. Firestone's tire solution involved 34-inch aluminum wheels which carried lightweight 48-inch diameter tires and were tested in Firestone's own laboratory.

The Flying Caduceus was barely ready for Bonneville in 1960, and a few runs were made uncovering some design and execution shortcomings. Flying Caduceus returned to The Salt in 1962 and in 1963 was clocked at 359.7mph. It never set a Land Speed Record.

But it did set a record for ingenuity, imagination and determination. 

A whole fleet of jet-powered cars followed the Flying Caduceus: the Arfons brothers, Craig Breedlove's Spirit of Americas, Gary Gabelich's Blue Flame, Richard Noble's Thrust and Andy Green's Thrust SSC.

They were all legendary, nearly miraculous accomplishments that inspired their competitors to do better, but all were in a direct chain that followed from Dr. Nathan Ostich's 1960 Flying Caduceus, the pioneer of jet-powered Land Speed Record attempts. It proved tire manufacturers like Firestone could build tires that would withstand the incredible forces of 500mph.

Flying Caduceus proved it was possible and that American hot rodders could build such a momentous machine.

It is today in largely original condition still with its Firestone Bonneville tires and is accompanied by a display General Electric J-47-19 turbojet engine.

The Flying Caduceus is one of a kind.

THE CAR OFFERED

The Volkswagen Karmann Ghia combined the dependable mechanical foundation of the Beetle with elegant Italian styling to create one of the most distinctive sporting automobiles of its era. Introduced in 1955, the Type 14 was penned by Carrozzeria Ghia and hand-assembled by German coachbuilder Karmann, transforming Volkswagen's utilitarian platform into a graceful grand touring coupe and, from 1957, a convertible. Its flowing bodywork has long been noted for its resemblance to Virgil Exner's Chrysler D'Elegance and K-310 concept cars, both of which Ghia had helped realize. 

While performance remained modest, the Karmann Ghia's balanced handling, refined styling, and everyday practicality earned it worldwide popularity, securing its place as one of the most enduring automotive designs of the postwar period.

This example early 1968 model, built in 1967, is finished in its original color combination of Gobi Beige with Khaki Brown upholstery and a black soft top. The body has benefited from a sympathetic repaint while remaining faithful to its factory colors, and the interior retains much of its original character, including the original upholstery with replacement seat cushions. The original soft top remains in place. A particularly desirable feature is its set of Riviera wheels, believed to be the original wheels from the dealership when new, a rare and highly sought after option among Karmann Ghia enthusiasts. Also accompanying the car is its original factory radio, currently not fitted.

Displaying an honest, well-preserved patina, this attractive convertible is reported by the owner to run well and comes with receipts of a full tuneup and service, making it an appealing example of Volkswagen's stylish coachbuilt classicâa symbol of the 1960s counterculture, often associated with freedom and style.

THE CAR OFFERED

This Silver Wraith Special Touring Limousine is one of only a handful of examples to be delivered with body style number 408 from Park Ward. A long wheelbase example of the second series of the model, it is thusly fitted with the more reliable 4,566cc straight six. This example, serial number ALW5, was ordered new as a factory demonstrator and VIP transport for Glascow, Scotland division of Rolls-Royce. Specified as a 7-passenger limousine, it was the first Silver Wraith bodied in Design no. 408. 

Introduced in May of 1952 and produced through September of 1953, a mere eight cars would be so bodied before style was replaced with the slightly different Design no. 551 in October 1953. According to copies of the factory build records, this car was finished in the understated but regal combination of Black over Biege leather up front and Fawn cloth in the rear. It would remain in the Glaswegian Rolls-Royce company motor pool for many years before eventually making its way to the United States. 

A California car for some time, it was in the Palm Springs garage of Robert Jerald Hill for the best part of three decades from January 1981 until the entering the current collection in 2008. A restoration project at the time of purchase, it was fully restored and modernized. The car is reported to have been completed disassembled, stripped to bare metal, and rebuilt. Repainted in two-tone metallic claret and silver, the interior was retrimmed in light grey leather up front and broadcloth in the rear with matching claret carpets piped in light grey. Modern air conditioning and stereo was installed along with an A/V system in the rear. Since completion, the car has been sparingly used. Most recently, it has been in dry storage for a few years with minimal use.

Accompanied by copies of its Rolls-Royce build sheets and Rolls-Royce Owner's Club records, the car is featured in Rolls-Royce: The Classic Elegance and Rolls-Royce Silver Dawn & Silver Wraith, each of which feature pictures of the car in period. This pickup is an early example of the sixth-generation F-100, introduced in 1973 and known to collectors as the "Dent side" for the pressed character line running the length of each body side. New for 1973 was a wider, more squared-off front end, a taller grille, and a more pronounced clamshell hood with reinforced internal bracing to reduce shake. The redesigned bodysides also relocated the front turn signals above the headlamps for the first time in Ford light-truck history, and the fuel tank was moved from behind the cab to beneath the bed floor as a safety measure â a change requiring a longer, wider frame and revised rear leaf springs to suit. The wheelbase grew two inches over the prior generation, and the new Style side bed was billed at the time as the widest in the industry. Underneath, Ford carried over the proven chassis and Twin-I-Beam independent front suspension dating to 1965, prioritizing continuity and durability even as the cab and sheet metal were thoroughly modernized.

This example is further optioned in Ranger XLT trim, the range-topping specification for 1973 and the F-100's most comfort-oriented offering. Ranger XLT equipment included color-keyed quilted cloth-and-vinyl seat upholstery, wood-tone-accented door panels and instrument-panel trim, wall-to-wall color-keyed carpeting with a carpeted behind-seat storage area, additional sound insulation, a color-keyed vinyl headliner, and a "Convenience Group" comprising cargo, engine, and glovebox lighting, a lockable glovebox, and a day/night inside mirror â appointments that, at the time, brought F-Series comfort levels closer to a Ford sedan than to a traditional work truck.

According to its door tag, this F-100 was manufactured in November 1972, an early-production example for the 1973 model year, and was assembled at Ford's San Jose, California plant. The VIN decodes to a 2-wheel-drive F-100 originally equipped with the 360ci V8. GVWR is rated at 5,000 lbs., with front and rear axle weight ratings of 2,850 and 2,836 lbs. respectively.

Preserved well beyond what is typical for surviving examples of the era, the truck has been sympathetically fitted with a Kelsey-Hayes automatic electric trailer brake controller, a Pioneer AM/FM/Bluetooth stereo, and Sparkomatic speakers, presenting a genuine survivor that remains fully ready to work.
